text: A Burlington correspondent relates the following incident that happened to him last week in a sleeping car on an American railway : We had taken in passengers for the night, the latest being from the backwood district. "We were all in bed in our respective recesses, when an inhabitant of one of the recesses started out with a terrific— " Gu-r-r-t I" That opened every eye in the car. We all hoped it was an accident, however, and, trusting that he wouldn't do it again, we all forgave him. Then he blasted our hopes and curdled the sweet serenity of our forgiveness by a long drawn " Gw-a, h h-h-hah ! " That sounded too much like business to be accidental. Then every head in that sleepless sleeper was held on the pillow for a minute, waiting, in breathless suspense, to hear the worst, and the sleeper in "lower three" went on in long drawn, regular cadences, that indicated good staying quali ties, " Gwa-a-ah ! Gwa-a-ah ! Gahwahwah ! G'ah wahwah ! Gawha•a-a-ah ? " Evidently it was going to last all night, and the weary heads drooped back on the sleepless pillows, and the swearing began. It mumbled along in low muttering tones, like dis tant echoes of a profane thunderstorm. Pretty soon "lower three" gave us a variation. He shot off a spiteful " Gwook ! " which sounded as though his nose had got mad at him, and was going to strike. Then there was a pause, and then we bean to hope hat he had either awakened from the sleep or strangled to death, nobody cared particularly which. But he disappointed everybody with a guttural " Gurroch " Then he paused again for breath, and when he had accumulated enough for his purpose, he resumed with a stentorian " Kowpf 1" that nearly shot the roof off the car. Then he went on playing such fantastic tricks with his nose, and breathing things that would make the immortal gods weep if they did but hear him. Just as the other passengers had consulted together how they might slay him, morning dawned. "lower number three" awoke. Everbody watched the curtains to see what manner of man it was that made that beautiful sleeping car a pandemonium. Presently the toilet was completed, the curtains parted, and "lower number three" stood revealed. Good heavens! It was a fair young girl, with golden hair and timid pleading eyes, like a hunted fawn's!"

text: ACCIDENT TO • KNOWLE RESIDE:T.—On Friday evening, Arthur Price, of Manor Farm, Widley, near Knowle, was driving in a trap along the Handsworth tramway route, when the wheels of his vehicle got fastened in the metals, and before they could be extricated a tram car came into collision with the trap. Price was thrown out of the trap and kicked about the ribs by the horse. He was taken to the General Hospital and detained, as he was suffering from several severely fractured ribs. ANNCAL VENISON DINNER.—On Friday, Sep tember the 11th, the annual venison dinner was held at the Greswolde Arms, Knowle. This dinner has the distinction of being one of the very few local institutions which have successfully resisted the levelling influences of time and change. For one hundred and fourteen years the dinner has been held annually, and now, owing to the exer tions of Mr. Morrill, it appears to have received a new leate of life, and promises well for the future. Although the weather was unsettled about seventy ' gentlemen sat down to dinner, being the largest attendance known for many years. The haunch of venison was, as usual, supplied by the Right Hon. Lord Leigh, and Mr. Morrill's catering was excellent. R. Ramsden, Esq., of Chadwick Manor, presided ; and A. L. Gibson, Esq., occupied the vice-chair. Among those present we noticed Messrs. Sanderson, F. Pope, J. J. Kimbell, H. Field, F. Field, J. Wilson, G. Wilson, A. Morrill, Dr. Hardwick, Adcock, Pearson, Be,anfoy, G. Hicken, Freeman, C. Kimbell, J. Wakefield, Rudd, T. Willcox, Barrett, Lovill, Dexter, W. Hardwick, G. Thompson, T. Glover, Gray, Lucas, Linguard, Frander, E. King, Battler, Green, &c. Letters of apology were read by the Chairman from Canon Howe (Vicar of Knowle) and Captain Boultbee, of Springfield, who were unable to be present in consequence of family bereavements. After the Chairman had proposed the usual loyal toasts, the Vice Chairman gave the health of Lord Leigh, which, it is hardly necessary to say, was received with great cordiality.—Mr. Ramsden next proposed "Success to the Venison Feast," and in an able and exhaustive speech, which was loudly applauded, traced the foundation of the dinner to a desire which existed among country gentlemen to afford encouragement to English sports. He then proceeded to show the good effects that English sports had had in forming the manly qualities of Englishmen, and concluded by expressing a fervent hope that whatever changes might take place, the legitimate sports of Englishmen might always be preserved.—The Chairman next proposed "Our Host," and Mr. Morrill, in reply, thanked the company present for their kindness in attending, and by so doing assisting him in his efforts to revive the dinner and place it upon its old footing.—During the evening some capital songs were rendered by many of the gentlemen, which added greatly to the enjoyment of the proceedings. The health of the Chairman and the Vice-Chairman having been duly honoured, a most enjoyable evening came to a close.

text: ALLEGED MURDER BY A SOLDIER. —ln Shorncliffe Camp, on Saturday evening, two private soldiers, named Morgan and Fonlstone, both bandsmen in the 82nd Regiment, were sitting in a hut with two drum mer boys. Morgan gave the boys some money to pur chase sweets, and they left the hut for that purpose. Almost directly afterwards Foulstone ran out of the but and into the next one with a frightful gash across his throat. He sank into a chair, and made signs for pen and ink. THE POISONING AT ELETEAD.—An enquiry was opened on Saturday, ou the bodies of Mr. and Mrs. Chandler and their son, who died through arsenical poisoning, at the Woolpack Inn. The Coroner said it seemed to him a very serious thing, and one which ought to be corrected, that a man could obtain so easily such a large quantity of arsenic. Had the law bearing on the sale of poison, which provided that arsenic should contain a certain admixture of indigo to colour it, been properly carried out, he did not see how it could have been mistaken for flour. From the evidence it appeared that the arsenic mixed in the pudding which Chandler and his family ate was sufficient to cause the death of at least fifty persons. Mrs. Chandler died within three hours afterwards, her eldest son at seven the same evening, and her husband at half.past one the next morning. The daughter who prepared the dinner re. sided with bar husband at the inn, and both escaped being poisoned under singular circumstances, the former being too unwell to eat any dinner, and the latter not returning home till later than usual. The inquiry stood adjourned till Wednesday, when the subject of the sale of the arsenic will be gone into. Two of Chandler's children are still in ft precarious condition. text: About four o'clock on Thursday afternoon, Samuel Cooke, aged forty-seven' of Halebank-terrace, Ditton, and employed as a clerk at Gaskell Deacon's chemical works, Widnes, made a determined attempt , to ccm mit suicide by jumping from Runcorn Bridge into the Manchester Ship Canal. The under side of the bridge is 75 feetabove high water,and Cooke's leap was fully 85 feet. Cooke was seen by several men on the banks of the canal and on the Transporter Bridge works to mount the rails of Runcorn Bridge, and without hesitation, jump off and drop like a stone into the water.--He sank, but after so long a drop he quickly rose to the surface, and he struggled most vigorously, in the meantime Mr. Szubbs, boatbuilder to Messrs. Abel; Mr. Richard Aspey, the ferryman; and Mr. Charles Wood had put off in a boat, and quickly reached the drowning man, and hauled him on board with a boathook. He was landed at Abel's Yard, and carried into a hut, where Police-constable Preston, Mr. W. Booth, and others applied artificial respiration. Detective Mottershead arrived on the scene with the ambulance car and some blankets. Mr. Cooke wa stripped, and placed in the blankets, and attended to by Dr. M`Lennan, who stated he was suffering from shock, but that there were no bones broken. Afterwards Detective Mottershead and Police-constable Preston removed Mr. Cooke to the Cottage Hospital. There is no doubt of Mr. Cooke's motive in making this desperate leap. Fastened to his coat by a long piece of string was a small, wide-necked bottle, such as is used in chemical laboratories, and in this bottle was the following remarkable letter ;—"I feel no fear. I commit my body to the water and my soul to my Maker, as I offered it to Him last night." It appears that on Thursdayafternoon, at his office in Gaskell Deacon's works, Mr. Cooke made his will, and had it witnessed by two office boys. Heaftervvards left the building, and did not return. In his drawer was found this will and a sheet of note paper on which were the words "Runcorn Bridge." It appears that Mr e Cooke has been very depressed lately owing to family troubles, and had recently consulted a doctor.

text: Captain Lindh, of the Swedish barque Architect, of Helsenburg, which arrivedonTuesday at Queens town, reports having been in close company with a large balloon for a short time in mid-ocean at nine o'clock at night on the 14th ult. The balloon was well inflated with gas at. the time; but how many persons occupied seats in the ear Captain Lindh cannot say, as darkness prevented him from ascer taining. He states that while on deck with all the crew he saw a balloon travelling rapidly through the air. It was bearing down on them, and was only 20ft. above the level of the sea. Captain Lindh first intended to make preparations to cap ture it and rescue the occupants from their very dangerous position, but on consideration it was decided not to run the risk. The balloon was wafted speedily with a fresh south-west breeze until it almost touched the vessel. It had long and stout ropes hanging out from the car, with grappl ing irons attached. These were dragged through the water, and greatly retarded the progress of the balloon through the air. If the ropes of the grappling irons had come across the spars of the Architect, a capture could have been made and the unlucky occupants rescued; but the balloon, which appeared with all its gear to be in perfect working order, was soon wafted out of sight, and was not seen afterwards. Captain Lindh said that, judging from the way the winds had been blowing since he had sailed from Florida, the balloon had been blown off the coast of Newfoundland, and it was reasonable to conclude that when the occupants realised this they let off an escape of gas and threw out their grapplings with the hope of striking one of the numerous fishing vessels off that coast.

text: Finding all complete at half-past twelve, and un willing to risk the balloon and exhaust the men by remaining longer en the earth, Mr. Simmons called for his campagnon de voyage. Sir Claude with sonse little difficulty made his way through the mass of men and took his seat in the car. The gigantic balloon was at this time surging and straining to and fro, threatening with every gust of wind to overpower the men, or to carry them all bodily into the air. Ex. ternal bags of sand were unhooked, and while the balloon was still fairly in the middle of the paddock, the aeronaut, it is said, gave the word, and Mr. Waller the signal whistle, to leave go Had this been implicitly and simultaneously obeyed, there can be little doubt that the " Colonel" and his freight would have cleared the wall and adjacent housetope, and have sailed freely and easily away into ethereal space. As badluck would have it, several of the men stuck with grim tenacity to the edge of the car, though carried completely off their feet, and in no small danger of being borne aloft. Having, however, shaken off the main power of restraint, but being still partially shackled, the balloon, carried by a stiffish whiff of the northeaster, went in an instant direct for the wall, and, to the horror of the people, came into un questionably violent collision with the coping, knocking off a couple of feet from the top layer. Sir Claude de Crespigny was at this time seated in the stern of the car facing the aeronaut, who was standing at the opposite end hauling the ropes. On receiving the first blow, which made the wickerwork of the oar creak audibly, and seemed for a moment to stagger the balloon. The "Colonel" made a slight rebound, and on this the passenger was seen to rise from his seat and seize the ropes. Instantaneously the car struck again, grazing the wall two feet lower than before. Sir Claude as now observed to put his foot on the edge of the car, and w he ther of his own volition or in response to cries of "come out," was assumed to be attempting to leave the balloon. The ear on receiving the second blow lurched forward. Sir Claude fell back among the men near the car. The two collisions and the fall from the car were all but instantaneous. More hands being laid on the balloon it was pulled down and dragged again to the middle of the paddock, but still swayed somewhat riskily, while Sir Claude, evidently in pain, lay on his back on the grass. He declared his leg was broken, and asked Captain Humphries, who was holding it, to put it down, and send for a hurdle. Mr. Gutteridge and Mr. T. Tomlinson, sur geons, attended him.. A little brandy was obtained, which, however, he declined to drink. A shutter was brought, on which he was taken to the house of Mr. Gutteridge, in the town.

text: General Booth, the veto : an head of the Salvation Army and one of the greatest figures in the religious and social work of our time, visited Warrington on Sunday and addressed two meetings in the Hippodrome. Although he has just attained his eighty-third year, the General still enjoys a remarb able degree of activity, and his presence inspires his soldiers with enthusiastic devotion. There is some thing pathetic in the knowledge that he is not able to see a single member of the huge audiences he addresses, for one of his eyes has had to be removed and there is a cataract in the other. At the end of this month the General is to undergo an opera tion which, in his own words, is to restore his vision and make a young man of him With characteristic cheeriness be gave his word that Ile had made up his mind to live as long as he possibly could and when Alderman Tinnion, in proposing a vote of thanks, made allusion to the General's " declining" vests, the veteran rose and deprecatingly interjected the words " Steady, now ! " With his flowing white hair end long beard, he looked a picturesque, venerable leader of men, and, although his voice teems to have got a little WE aker since last he visit e d HP, he spoke with all his wonted fervour nod conviction ?bout the splendid work of the mar vellous orpardsation which he brought into being. The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) presided at the afternoon -fleeting and amongst thove on the platform were ! Aldermen A. Bennett, W. Pierpoint, D. Tinnion, James Evans and J. Smethurst, Councillors W. H. J. Jenkins, J. Dickenson, T. S. Steel and J. T Locker, Mrs. Garnett (renketh), Mrs. Withinshsw, Mr. and Mrs. J. A. Ransome, Mr. W. H. Woo-'ccck and Mr. T. Prince. The MAYOR said the organization which General Booth had instituted and built up was highly valued as a great influence in the many countries to which it had penetrated. He would liken the Salvation Army to those whom the Master, in the parable of the Feast, sent out into the highways and byways to compel the lame, the halt and the blind to come in. It was the function of the Army to shed the light of Christianity upon those who would never think of attending a place of worship. The recent Titanic disaster, by the heroism and self-sacrifice which it called forth, had shown how men were capable of living noble and use ful lives and if E 0 many heroes were to be found amongst a concourse of 2,000 people how many inore i potential heroes must tly . re be n the world, waiting for a body like the Salvation Army to induce them to make the best of their lives. (Applause). General BOOTH, who was warmly applauded on rising to speak, said a great change had com e over the public mind during the last few years with reference to the work and character of the movement, but some very peculiar notions still prevailed. It was not long since the General of-the Salvation Army was commonly repre sented as an autocratic despot, ruling his people with rod of iron. Those who Mile such statements failed to tell them that the General was perhaps the best beloved leader of any religious or philan thropic movement on the face of the earth (Applause.) It was commonly believed that General Booth was a splash adventurer, piling up a colossal fortune for himself and for his family. Those who made that statement f a il e d t o say that General Booth during the forty-Enven years the Salvation Army bad existed had never taken a shilling from its coffers for his own support. (Applause.) Much was mid of the magnificent mansion in which the General reAded and the splendid motor car in which he rode about the world but no witness was ever produced who had ever seen the mansion or the motor. Then there was a great deal of talk about tbe want of prope- accounts and balance sheets, although as a fact there was perhaps no religious or philanthropic movement on the face of the earth that took so-much pains and spent so much labour on its statements as to the income and expenditure of its /nods. lie cure heard a man who complained "What a pity General Booth does not issue a balance sheet."

Just before the train moved away the general stepped out upon the platform qf the drawing room car, when he was loudly cheered by the crowd. According to arrangements, the general, who was accompanied by Mrs. and Miss Grant, travelled from Manchester in a special train, which, leaving the Northern capital at noon, arrived at' St. Pancras at half-past four. text: Little attention has been bestowed of late years upon the vagaries of the cyclist by the police, who have had their hands full trapping bigger game in the persons of motorists. But it behoves cyclists not to be lulled into false security, for a haul of cyclists, some thirty-one riders, were fined for furious cycling a few weeks ago at the North London Police Court. Some of the victims were ladies, who explained with surprise that they were not riding at 20 miles an hour. But the magis trate pointed out to them that there was no question of a speed limit for cycling, and that under certain circumstances five miles an hour might be considered dangerous. It usually happens that trie police take action against cyclists only when moved thereto by local complaints respecting inconsid.mta riding/ The Superiority of the Cycle over the motor-cycle and the small car was forcibly brought home to me last week when I formed one of a party of five on a combined motor-cychw and photographing tour. One small car, one motor cycle, and one push bicycle were used, and the journey covered about 600 miles. The car wanted repairs or attention about once in every 50 miles, the motor-cycle once in 150 miles, but the only repairs wanted by the push bicycle in the 600 miles had to do with one burst tyre, which took ten minutes to mend. text: On Saturday Birkenhead was favoured with a visit from tho members of the Northern Section of the Incorporated British Institute of Certified Carpenters and their friends, and as the weather was ideal a very pleasant day was spent in the district. There are some 24 members of the Institute in this locality, whilst in the Northern Section, comprising Yorkshire, ,Lancashire, Durham, Cheshire and Derby shire, there is a membership numbering only about 40. The party met in the morning at Liver pool Landing Stage and crossed to New Ferry, the training ships and Atlantic liners proving objects of great interest to the friends from other places. At New Ferry wagonettes were in attendance, and a very pleasant drive was taken to Lever Brothers' works. The works and the chief buildings in the garden town were in spected with interest, and the party then walked to the car terminus, and thence travelled to Birkenhead, alighting at Abbey-street. The old Priory ruins were inspected, and the company then repaired to the Higher Elementary Schools, Conway street, where tea was partaken of. An adjournment wavafterwards made to the lecture room, where an excellent lec ture on "Architecture in relation to Car pentry" was given by Mr. F. 0. Creswell (hon. fellow), before the members and stu dents of the school. Mr. James Merritt presided, and in hie own name and that ef his fellow townsmen he gave the visitors a hearty welcome to Birkenhead. He said he wished to thank the members of the Association for the good work they had done, were doing, and which he ho they would continue to do. He thought e was in a position to speak of the value of technical knowledge. He did not think the education authorities gave this subject anything like the considera tion and attention which it deserved. He hoped that before long greater facilities and inducements would be held out to the young men to get them to take up the study of the scientlic part of their business. The lecture was given by Mr. Creswell in a very masterly way, proving that he had the subject at his finger ends. The paper, which was illustrated with admir able, and in many cases beautiful, slides, dealt with many kinds of architecture. Votes of thanks were afterwards heartily accorded to the lecturer, the Chairman, and lanternist. The proceedings were brought to a close by a private conference of the members.

text: Probably the reason why so many of the trial cars are so frequently seen out of adjustment lies in the fact that each one is driven, at various times, by three or four different drivers. Hence, when anything goes wrong, the natural impulse of the man who has little interest in his work is to get back to the depot as best he can and leave the trouble of the adjustments or repairs to the next man who takes the car out. This one speedily finds that matters are wrong, but argues that he is not going to put things right for others, so he, too, manages as best he can and trundles the car out and back again by a series of makeshift devices. A practical foreman would speedily put a stop to such manceuvring; but, unfortunately,many of the men who hold this responsible position are not practical, and so in tpis way business is lost, cars are spoilt and the reputation of.the firm is ruined solely through the laziness and the incapacity of its employees.

text: Recent news from the Scottish Women's Hospitals in France and Serbia, organised by the Scottish Federation of the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, more than justifies the enterprise and courage of those noble women who initiated the venture. text: THE EFFECT OF MAL-ALIGNMENT. It is an accepted fact that a combina tion outfit is constructed contrary to scientific principle. This is allowed for by makers, in that the material used is sufficiently strong to withstand the. severe strain which is imposed on the frame of the cycle. If, however, the wheels are not in true alignment the strain is increased enormously,and this additional strain will seriously effect the running of the machine as a whole. There are two things to look for when testing the alignment. The three wheels should be vertical, and the side car wheel should be parallel to the cycle wheels. If .found incorrect it is an easy matter to adjust them by altering the couplings. The tyres on a badly aligned machine, moreover, wear out con siderably quicker than is the case when the wheels are true. PROTRUDING TRAMLINES. • •

text: The Meet of the Coaching Club on the Saturday before the Derby is an event of the season. Grave doubts beset the path of the committee who had charge of the arrangements, willing but unable, to make any terms with the clerk of the weather. But fortune favoured the brave, and in a glow of delicious sunshine, with the park in richest beauty, and thousands of spectators lining the roadway, the lint coach drew Up at the Magazine at half past 12 o'clock. There is a fashion in coaches as in other social hobbies, in their colour and little details of their turn-out. For two or three years vermilion and Indian red were the prevailing colours for wheels and window panels. Here and there a yellow coach would relieve the sombre, and tone down the obtrusive, colours, but never more than three of this very advancing tone, in a day's muster. Now yellow is all the rage, and the meet chewed 11 out of 19 coaches in this colour. Four shades were to be noted, one of a deep cadmium, not far removed from orange, several of primrose, one or two of the old-fashioned lemon, and one of the faint lines only of yellow with blue lines picking out. The ladies on the roofs looked very picturesque, in spite of the necessity for wearing high-shouldered circular cloaks. One or two wore tailor-made tweed without any muffle, and yellow vest and flowers, to match the painting of the coach. Bonnets were more worn than hats, but with both of than black was the popular head-covering,with brilliant lowers. The new geranium colour is an effective shade for brightening up the group of broad-clothed tentlemen of a coaching party. In the smart equipages to be noted in the West End during the last month we see the hones with broad forehead bands of strong yellow with glazed surface, or else of crimson lace, but always in harmony with the liveries. The side rosettes are diminished in size; possibly it is the broad forehead band that seems to dwarf the size of the rosettes. Last year a number of ends of ribbon fluttering from the rosettes were the fashion, like recruiting sergeants' ribbon cut short. This year these ends have disappeared, and only the rosette remains. With the Belli cars flowers deck the horses car, and the hone-band is plated, or else made of plain, untanned leather. AURORA.

text: The Picture Post Card.—At no time of the year does the picture post card play a more useful part than during the holiday season. No doubt its popularity depends to some extent upon its frivolity, as many people spend a great deal of their time in hunting out and purchasing cards with satirical suggestions relating to the hobbies or weaknesses of their friends to whom the cards are sent. It is a harmless way of providing fan for the breakfast table, but the great merit of the picture card is, that it enables us to keep on good terms with our friends with out making a burden of one's correspondence. The old-fashioned letter of several pages closely written, and crossed, has in fact almost disappeared, except perhaps amongst the community of old maiden aunts. With the great majority of people the picture card serves sufficiently for all epistolary requirements, and our thanks are due to the person who tint invented this very useful means of saving us time and trouble, About Luggage.—The holidays are making it very clear that, as a nation, we have still further improved in the matter of luggage. The battered tin box is an item of the past, neat leather portmanteaux, or Glad stone bags of wicker covered in canvas, having taken its place. Then there are the useful expanding wicker baskets, into which an almost incredible amount of clothing can be packed. Elaborately fitting dressing bags are rarely seen nowadays, the unfortunnte owners having discovered that the majority of the fittings are more or less useless, and that when packed such a bag requires a man and a boy to lift it. The Safest Place in a Train.—With the holiday season in full swing, there is usually not much choice as re- • gards any particular seat in a train. The carriages are so crowded that it is usually a case of getting in where one can, and there is no opportunity to consider which is the safest seat on the train. The question, however, is often asked by travellers, and an expert gives it as his opinion after careful calculation, that the safest place is in the middle of the last car but one. There are some risks he says which are the same in every part of the train, but others which are less at this particular spot. It is not of course always possible to pick and choose, but those who are nervous about rail v;aytravelling might bear in mind that a centre seat is safer than a corner one and so also is a centre com partment, as compared with the end compartment of a car._ _ .

text: The village of Studley, Warwickshire, has been the scene of most disgraceful confusion, occasioned by the marriage of an old man, named Joshua Davis, to a girl named Cashmore. The bridegroom, a widower, I. said to be sixty-eight year. of age, and the bride but little over fourteen, the former being possessed of some mean*, and the latter the daughter of poor labouring marmite. The banns had been duly pub lished, and every effort bad been made to induce Davis from carrying out his intention, or, at least, to let the event take place quietly at some other than holiday time, but all to no purpose. He ma. determined on the incongruous alliance, and the in habitants of Studley, equally determined to show their indignation, assembled at the church to witness the proceedings in large numbers. They strewed the path from the church gates to the doors, and through the porch, with thorns, briars, nettles, old tin kettles, old shoes, and other refuse, while tin kettles were loudly beaten, and other marks of disapprobation made. The •icar and churchwardens met the car conveying the old man and his bride some distance from the church, and again remonstrated with him, but all to no purpose. The car and pair of greys arrived at the church gates about half past nine, ai»id deafening yells, hisses, and groans, and as the pair passed into the church the old man was pelted with rotten eggs, tufts of grata, and other missiles. Scarcely a word of the ceremony could be heard for the din and confusion that prevailed in the church. Occasionally groans, and cries of "Now, Joshua," were to be distinguished among the uproar. The service over, the people hurried from the church to prepare for giving the old man a warm reception, which they did by repeating the dose of rotten eggs, &c., whilst the groans and yells of the people, coupled with the solemn tolling of the bells.. if for a funeral, made a scene long to be remembered. The old man, evidently fearing personal violence, rushed into the car, and left his youthful wife, who wore& wreath and veil, and, in spite of the tumult, looked all smiles and happiness, among the crowd, whose indignation ap peared to be levelled at the aged bridegroom only. A. further warm reception awaited the bralegroom at his noose, where numbers of people had assembled, and where the previous scenes were repeated.

text: This ancient village, BOOTHTOWN and its modern and AND THE tasteful adjunct, TRAMWAYS. Akroydon, have now been brought into the great tramway fellowship that is rapidly enclosing every corner of the Borough. In no district is it likely that the cars will be more heartily supported than by the hard-working and oft weary hill climbers of Boothtown and the hamlets beyond. "It's a rare lift" ! is the oft heard expression of the occupants of the cars, and no doubt the thought of the weary worker will oft-times revert to the time when after his or her day's labour the fatigue was prolonged and increased by the climb on foot from North Bridge to Ploughcroft, to say nothing of the expense it sometimes caused, when the steepest " bit " could hardly be faced without a little " soop-o'-gooid " at " th' Cooach," which would perhaps be followed by a little reminiscence at the "Dutchman." Now a-days the weariness is relieved instead of being increased on the way home, and the cost, deducting the price of the aforesaid " soop " and the following " reminiscence," is, as the Irishman would say, about threepence less than nothing. The most frequently-heard name up that way seems to be "Michael." Whether Archangel, Saint, Alderman or Justice, the people never trouble to say—it is simply plain "Michael." He is evidently somebody who is reverently and thankfully looked up to as having, by well-directed persistency, done a great deal towards securing a tramway service for Boothtown, but as we didn't care to expose our ignorance we never ventured to make any further inquiries respecting the identity of the mysterious personage whom the Booth towners unanimously call "Michael " simply that and nothing more. If a statue is ever erected to the gentleman we would strongly urge that the inscription should be simply " Michael," surrounded by a wreath of tram-rail, and surmounted by a car. Anything else would be super fluous and spoil it.

There had been, he said, a diminution in the number of commercial law cases tried in the Law Courts, which might have arisen from the desire of commercial men to have disputes settled more rapidly and cheaply than by going to law. For centuries the Skis, or the Norwegian snow-ehom, which, by-the-tye, are quite a different thing from the esumeien coos--shoe (Black and White explains) have been the serest, and easiest means of locomotion in that hilly and snow bound country during the long and dark winter months. The Skis are long, flat wooden rminers, about set-en or eight feet long, six inches wide, and from half to three-quarters of an inch thick, made of various kinds of elastic wood, and with gracefully turned-up euds in front. They are fas tened to the feet by one or two leather straps, and with an Alpine staff and a tair of thick woollen socks, Form the necessary outfit of the Ski-runner. It is difficult to imagine a finer sight than that of a Ski runner, on a frosty winter day, rushing at liehtning pace down the mountain side past the green pine and fir trees—a sight at which our cyclists would sie , ply stand aghast and envious, willing, no doubt, to exchange, there and then, their stylish iron " bike' for these two simple pieces of wood, if they were only sure of the necessary accessories for this exhilarating sport—plenty of snow and bills. Even the ladies have joined the ranks of the Ski runners, and have performed the most extraordinary feats in running and jumping. Within the last few years, annual races, or competitions, have been estab lished. text: As I anticipated a short time ago, Ladies to the Front. this is going to be a ladies' year. They are coming on with a rush, and taking to cycling as ducks take to water. There is a big demand for machines to suit. I expect that in this, as in so many other matters, we self-styled lords of creation will have to go to the wall. It will be a bit, however, before Mrs Grundy sanctions their appearance in tights on the cinder track. Yet why not there, as well as behind the footlights. on Thursday were booked for Annan. The threatening weather might account for the fact of only six turning up. One who took part in the run tells me that as they were all good goers, they arranged to go on to Dumfries. The weather in the outward journey was dry, but there was a strong steady head wind, so that it took 1 hour 45 minutes to reach Annan (17 miles). From Annan they took the low road to Dumfries, which is 18 miles, one mile longer than the other route. This was done in the same time. After a wash and a meal at the Commercial Hotel, they prepared to take the road back, and found that it was raining. The captain, like the careful man that he is, produced a. cape and a mud guard, and as he was likewise the only man with a gearing case, he had the pull on all the rest. Some were without capes, and some with out mud guards, but some pieces of cardboard were provided, fixed to the middle tube, to catch the wash from the front wheel, and they answered the purpose well. The rain had stilled the wind, the road was one long canal. A steady stream of dirty water flew from the edge of the wheel, :plastering the hair with the mud which was flung up as high as the head. Not withstanding these adverse conditions, thdY reached Annan in 1 hour 35 minutes. After a short rest, the journey was once more resumed, and the second stage to Stanwix was accomplished in the same time as the first. That was 11 miles an hour, including stoppages for lighting lamps, adjusting chains, and so on. It rained the whole way., and those without capes had as a substitute, a coating of mud, about half-an-inch thick, from head to hip, where width depended on the breadth of the back that bore it. Two of the six were a long way behind at the finish. The necessity of adjusting their chains was the first cause of delay; then after leaving Annan they saw what they took to be an immense conflagration; a burning factory, or something equally sensational. They turned from the main road, and set off at full speed for the spot, their hearts, no doubt, beating high with generous emulation to do some noble and daring deed. Finally they came so near that only a field or two intervened. Their conviction that some terrible holocaust was in progress became stronger as the flames appeared to be surrounded by a crowd. They dismounted, and leaving their " bikes " in the hedge, stumbled across two ploughed fields, to find—a brick kiln—" Isn't this a sell," said one. "I think we had better go home," said his philosophic friend. They had one small mite of consolation, they were not the only ones sold. The kiln watchman informed them that a number of " travellers " who had made the kiln their resting place, had skedaddled under the impression that the detectives were upon them. too had only a small muster, owing The Co-operative to the threatening out-look of the weather. Their destination was Langholm, via Longtown, and Gretna, but on reaching the latter place, prudence prevailed. Signs of rain were too plain to be ignored, and a start was made homeward, timed so admirably, that Carlisle was reached just in time to escape a wetting. The annual sports promoted by this club will be held shortly, probaby the week after next, out Gretna way.

text: Devonshire and its roads..----We had to stay at Appledore a day longer than we had planned, on account of having advised some friends to address theit letters to Launceston by a certain date. As it was, we had to leave the little town a good deal sooner than we would have desired.lnstead of taking the direct Clovelly road, from Bideford, which was sure to be crowded with market carts and traps, coming in to Bideford Market, for Tuesday was market day, we sought a less crowded way up the little Yeo Valley, a tributary of the Torridge. There we found the procession just as bad, pei haps aggravated by the narrow road. S 9 for four miles we were dodging this traffic. Worse still a violent downpour came in the middle of it, and made two thuds of the road useless for cycle's. The drivers were politeness itself ; in every case they draw into the soft mess ate the side and left us as much ef the crown as they could. For tbr-y have a special recipe for road repairs there. "To two tons of road metal add three tons of road scrap ir,gs, sod parings, &c ; roll until the metal appears at the surface ; it is then ready for all kinds of traffic except modern vehicles." In a week or two, the road, say 24 feet wide is divided into three sections. he centre is fairly fit for riding on ; the other two-thirds is a mass of mud in wet weather, a depth of dust in dry, and wretched ruts in between wades. Devon shire roads are the worst we have seen in all England or Wales. You can rely on a week in the Devonshire combes pulling down your average, but the awful state of the roads added to their slope will make your cyclo meter ready to kick you out of the county. Before reaching Clovelly you ride three miles through the Hobby Drive and don't grudee the six pence, for it is a beautiful ride. All motors and waggonettes are stopped at the entrance; only the "push bike" may be ridden, and small gigs 'or traps allowed through. Tne surface is excellent; the gradients easy, and th e delightful shade of the trees is constant as the track winds around the sides of the ravines till it ends at the top of the staircase leading down to Clovelly harbour. It is no use taking the cycles down with you. As an Irishman might say, no one but donkeys can climb down to the sea or back again. But notwithstanding the crowds of trippers, and the notice boards announcing "Teas, lodging, or beds," Clovelly is beyond all words delightful, and on that sunny afternoon the flowers on all hands, yet dripping from the recent rain, made it appear Just like all Devonshire packed into one little bit of a sample. But there, Kingsley's description barely does it justice, so why throw away words on such a place. The place from which everyone should see Clovelly has been made accessible by the opening of the Hobby Drive. The view is unique, and that summer afternoon nothing could be more beautiful. The blue sea, the white cottages tumbling down to it, the grey harbour, the green forest, the purple cliffs beyond and Lundy Island lying far away—" see Clovelly and then When we reached the top of the moor above, the wind was for the first time at our hack, blowing North west. Before we reached Kilkharnpton on our way to Bude we had reason to bless the motor charabancs. Our "innards " were calling for tea, for the ups and downs of those Cornish moors (we were at least in Cornwall) break up the molecules of the last meal very quickly; a road-side farm announced " Good teas provided daily," and, inquiring, we were shown into the tea room. It was a sight that would have made a Sunday school tea-party's mouth's water, Stewed rasps and clotted cream "by the galore," six or eight different kinds of cake, flowers decorating every yard of table, teas Bet fer thirty or so, and all this miles from town or village. We asked the black and white young lady if we had intruded on some party's good fortune. "Oh no, we provide this every day," it was for the charabancs and coaches which always stop there on the road to Bude, Hartland, Clovelly, Bideford and other holiday centres, so we did justice to our " innnards " and were charged 9d. each. Our run for last Saturday was looked forward to, and a large turn-out was ex pected, our destination being Beeston Castle, but unfortunately at the time of starting the rain was coming down, and Mr. Brown and many others were conspi cuous by their absence. Fifteen started shortly after 3 p.m. Nearing Ledsham we bade adieu to a couple of our members who had other fish to fry at Rhyl. Chester was reached in good time, then on through Tar. yin to Tarporley. Here we were met by two of our members who had preceded us earlier on in the day, and had made ar rangements for tea. After tea we paid an in teresting visit to the eaves which are under the ground in various directions, close on 60 feet. Here the glee singers were heard at their best. Coming out in the daylight once more we climbed up to the ruins, where a splendid view is to be had of the surrounding country. The River Mersey is easily seen in the distance; a mile away stands Peckforton Castle, the seat of Lord Tollemache. Here we are told Oliver Cromwell placed his guns and lowered the walls of Beeston Caste. Our guide then takes us to the old well which is 6 feet in , width, and goes down to the level of the I roadway a depth of 366 feet; and was also used as a means of escape in olden daps, a passage half-way down the well leading out a mile away, but now blocked up. Our time is now up, and we reluctantly mount on bikes shortly after eight o'clock. Hooton being reachea, we rest for ten minutes, while some members recharged with petrol, etc. Here we were compli mented by a chauffeur on our idea of carry ing a red tail light, which might be more widely adopted by other clubs, who he says cannot be seen until the motor is almost on top of them. A slight spill in Easthain delayed us a while, then home, Seacombe being reached shortly before 11 o'clock after a meet instructive and enjoyable run, all finishing as fit as fiddles. text: Early on Friday morning we were Out sight seeing on our bikes. We visited the Place de la Concorde, the Champs Elysees, and went through the Arc de Triumph° to the Bois de Boulogne, where hundreds of cyclists, mostly ladies, were flitting among the trees of the boulevards, and the grace with which they rode their cross-frame machines would put to shame many English wheelmen. They, of course, almost all wore the rational dress, and very pretty indeed some of them appeared. Afterwards we rode to Longshamp, a noted racecourse, and then returned to our hotel at about 7-30. We gave our cycles a rest in the evening, and visited the place. of amusement. At one of the wonderful jardins, which are so numerous In the city, we were able to see Paris life at its gayest. On Saturday morning we visited many of the noted buildings of the town, including the opera house, Madeline, the Eiffel Tower, the Tuilleries, Palais de Justice, and Notre Dame. At the cathe dral we witnessed, with much interest, a French wedding, which was quite different to the English ceremony. In the streets we noticed a French funeral passing, and as the hearse passed a French man, no matter of what class, the man would stand still and reverently uncover his head until the vehicle had passed. The persons in the funeral procession also walked bare-headed. At three o'clock on Saturday we left the gay city en route for Rouen and Dieppe. After cycling part of the way we found darkness fast approaching, and in order to catch the midnight boat at Newhaven, we were compelled to take the train. The return by boat was much rougher than the passage from England, and soon some of our company were on I the sick list. We got to Newhaven at six o'clock on Sunday morning, and having exchanged our foreign money into English coins we rode along the coast to Brighton. The roads, of course, were a, pleasing change to those abroad, and we soon felt I we were in England once more, glad to be where I we could resume our own longtime and gratify our I own feelings once more in our own sweet way. Sunday we spent in Brighton, enjoying the sea-bath and promenading on the pier. We left Brighton on Monday morning and got to London, where we caught a through train to Manchester, and thus arrived home shortly after noon on Monday. Dur ing the entire journey we came off without any mishap to our cycles, none of the party even having I had a puncture, and throughout the tour we had, ' by cycle, boat, and train, travelled over 1,200 miles. I should not advise anyone contemplating a tour on the Continent to take their machines with I them. The roads are so very bad that it is only in the vicinity of the large towns that a bit of decent riding can be obtained. In the large cities the cafés and hotels all provide stands for cycles at the door, and in many cases large foot pumps are at the service of any cyclist in need. The fares from Nelson, for the machines alone, exceeded a sovereign, and we had a lot of trouble in getting I them booked, seeing them shipped, &c. In Holland, Belgium and France there is no charge made by the railway companies for conveying passengers' cycles, though there are a lot of formalities to go through. Formerly fees used to be charged as a deposit on cycles landing in Holland, which were returned on leaving the Continent. This system is now abolished, and our passports and club badges were sufficient to admit us without paying duty. I may say that abroad you are compelled to have your name and address on a plate fixed in a prominent place on your cycle. This we had done before leaving Nelson. In Holland and Belgium the railway carriages are considerably worse in their accommodation than the worst excursion train in Lancashire. We found the people, es pecially in Belgium, kind and obliging almost to excess. Every time we addressed a foreigner in the streets the men always politely raised his hat before speaking, and again before leaving us. Brussels was the best place we visited for fine buildings, cleanline:s and civility. The Frenchmen are not over scrupulous, and many a time we had to point out that the change was wrong. Then, with many excuses, the remainder of the money would be put down. Attempts were also made to give us bad money in change. The scenery through the country from town to town was very poor, and it is only the large towns that are worth visiting. In the country the labouring classes live in dirty sorts of houses and both men, women, and children go about barefooted and in very slovenly attire. A noticeable difference between foreign and our English country life

Accordingly I mounted my machine, which is a " Scout" and consequently of first rate order, and dropped through Huddersfield as quickly as possible. I was bound for Bradford, but was uncertain which way to go. Upon arriving at the " Three Nuns" I dismounted and asked the way to Cleckbeaton, staling that my ultimate destination was Bradford. My informant directed me through the village of Dartshead, across the moor by way of Scholes, Wyke, Low Moor, and down the hill to the town that has produced plenty of cloth, but it is said never has produced a county cricketer. I was much amused on the way at a little incident that occurred on Hartshead Moor. Feeling uncertain as to whether I was pursuing , the right road, I slackened my pace and shouted to a drowsy teamer who lounged in a coal cart on • pillows that were not white :—" Is this the way to Wyke " Be looked up in astonishment, grinned broadly and then I shouted my question again, and understanding me to ask " Is this the way to bike?" he assured me that I did fairly well. From Bradford I journeyed through beautiful Saltaire, charming Shipley, and picturesque Bingley, on my way to Keighley. I had met with innumerable cyclists, but up those dreadful streets not one dared to go. I dismounted, and mused whether it was that the Keighley town councillors did not cycle, or were interested in some cycle company that they preserved their streets in so wretched a condition. I was not astonished to hear some boys shout when I mounted again : -" Look, look, a man on a bike!" for I suppose the most natural •place there is off the machine. text: Many interesting opinions on this interesting question are contributed by well-known women of the day to the September number of "Pearson's Magazine!" among the writers being " Rita," Madame Albani, the late Lady Florence Dixie, Mrs. Farquharson of Haughton, and Una L. Silberrad. "Rita" says:—" The woman of the future? The woman of the next century. What a field for the imagination! Since she proclaimed herself emanci pated, since she threw off the control and limita tions of sex, woman has overthrown barrier after barrier, and now stands as man's equal in all things appertaining to work, sport, morals—or vices! For if gambling, betting, drinking, and smoking are not vices, they come within an appreciable distance of that description. Fifty years might see well a new generation, the product of the strange hybrid female who • golfs' and hockeys ' and 'bikes '—who motors, and steeplechases, and bets, and smokes; who is never at home unless obliged, and makes a club do duty for domesticity; who goes in for Stock Exchange gambles, and has a telephone service be tween boudoir and broker—who wants a place on the judge's bench and in the jury-box—who speaks with authority of all subjects from public platforms —to whom man is either a 'pal' or a slave—to whom wifehood is boredom and motherhood an in sufferable affront of Nature! The future woman will probably have inforced her right to vote and to legislate, judging from the recent disgraceful scenes of the Linsexed ' suffragette.' She will be the maker of strange and coatradictory laws. She will have a new code of morals, and will force illogical prob lems down the public throat. She will, in fact, be everything except a woman in the old time honoured reverent meaning of the word. The girl of the present day cares nothing for poetry, music, art, or literature. She prefers to live on the golf links or on the hockey fields—to ride a ' motor-bike ' —to follow the guns—to ape man in all his pursuits. If she marries it is to be free from parental control or parental objections—to go her own way, choose her own friends, have her own club and latch-key, and take unto herself 'spirits seven times worse than herself' as emancipated examples." Una Sil berrad, the well-known novelist, has other views. She writes: 'lt is rather difficult to prophesy with regard to women; they are so infinitely variable, so curiously influenced by surroundings —a rule that is more than half exceptions. But as far as it is pos sible to judge, it seems to me that the woman of the future will be more really man's equal than she is to-day. There is, I suppose, little doubt that the women of the middle and upper classes are hardly clear of an uncomfortable condition of transi tion. Some are still suffering from new liberties, undigested education, and a somewhat youthful re volt, in words at least, against the restraints of old fashioned religion, morality, and decorum. But in the lower classes it is all quite different. There women have had the right to earn bread for them selves or others as long as anyone can remember, and have not been the worm or the better house wives and mothers on that account. They have had education as ion* as their men have had it; not for very long certainly; but of much the same kind. It seems to me that this state of affairs must, in time, come in the higher classes too. Each sex will have to give up something of its exclusive privi leges; each will have to look the other squarely in the face and recognise not only the points of resem blance, but also the fundamental differences. But I believe it will come. I feel far more sure of it than that women will be paneled as a jury, or that they will free themselves from the sti gma of being the one tax-paying unrepresented section of the community."

text: THE future historian of the social life of Great Britain will not fail to notice and com ment upon the curious revival of bicycling which has been everywhere apparent during the past year. Not the least remarkable aspect of the circumstance is that, instead of being a new fad suddenly adopted by the public and likely to be as eagerly cast aside in favour of some succeeding caprice, cycling is really but a development of a slow and steady movement which has drawn the nation with it to such an extent that it seems destined to remain until some absolutely new method of locomotion is invented. We can lay claim to have manufactured the first velocipede, in the same way that the honour of the original steam engine is ours by right. But the continent has traded upon the happy idea, foreigners have adopted the wheel with an enthusiasm little dreamed of among un athletic people, and to some extent its latter resuscitation began abroad rather than at home. Certain it is that the popularisation of the bicycle for women is as much due to the Parisians as to any pioneers in a similar direction at home. In the history of feminine France, for the first time a means of healthy exercise has been widely adopted. The Sports in which Englishwomen delight—tennis, rowing, and golf—have signally failed to attract. Indeed, the point of view adopted by the Parisian in such matters has been that such sports are for men, and are unwomanly, as entailing upon the weaker sex exertions unfitted to its strength. The extraordinary zeal exhibited for "the cult of the cycle" abroad is therefore all the more remarkable, while the earnestness of purpose animating the female mind has rengered it proof against the arrows of ridicule which contemporary satire did not hesitate to launch against the movement in its incipient stages. There is still an enormous field left for bicycle enterprise, viewed both from the standpoint of the amateurs who mount their machines, and from that of the manufacturers who turn them out by the thousand from their factories. So far, it is satisfactory to note that the British-made article stands pre eminent among its competitors, and that, haying practically a monopoly of the beet marktts, for the present our makers are fully able to hold their own, even in the face of overwhelming Protective duties. The average bicyclist nowadays, if properly mounted, can cover as much ground in twenty-four hours as his forefathers took in four or five days; while figures latterly published disclose the fact that many a rider, if he wishes to travel in the South of England, had better put his legs across his machine than rely upon the speed of the so-called railway express. For similar reasons, the man who possesses a horse will be glad to supplement it with a bicycle, while the "upper ten," who once . denominated those who bestrode " bikes " as "cads on castors," are now everywhere learn ing to ride the people's machine, and learning to ride it well. Indeed, everything goes to . prove that the cycle is now a recognised and orthodox institution in our midst with high and low, and just as the locomotive has gradually been evolved from the derided ' Puffing Billy of Stephenson to the admired and perfect engine of to-day, so may we expect the bicycle, in the course of the next year or two, to attain to the degree of perfection which modern mechanical skill promises.

text: There were six of us. We were all Nelson I cyclists, being members of the Nelson C.C., and we ; decided to spend our August holidays and foarth • annual tour abroad, and on our bikes. There were such preparations! I forget the number of meet ings we had to arrange the week's programme, and then as the time for the holidays approached we took to rng before breakfast in order to be In the best of form. We arranged the details of the holiday very minutely, and each man was allotted a certain amount of the work connected with the arrangements. For instance, one man was ordered to pick up fragments of the French language, and ' he was to act as interpreter on the tour; another man had to make himself acquainted with the roads to be traversed; another with the hotels to be stayed at; another with the foreign coinage, and so on. Thus each man did his share of the work. There was only one repairing outfit for the whole six of us, and an effort was made to carry as little luggage as possible. We each took a change of linen with us, and this was placed in a bag attached to the machine. Through the instru mentality of Mr. R. M. Prescott, the town clerk, we obtained passports, which were signed by the Mayor (Councillor Reed). Thus it was that, after discussing the merits and demerits and one thing and another, we left Nelson, early on the morning of last Saturday week, by train to London. On arriving at St. Pancras we cycled across London to Waterloo Station, where we caught the 8-30 evening train for the continent, via Harwich. At half-past ten on Saturday night we left the shores of England, where after a couple of hours on board we adjourned to our berths for a sleep, but this was out of the question, for two members of the party would neither sleep them selves nor let anyone else who were near them; anyhow after a calm and pleasant sail we were in Dutch waters by six o'clock on Sunday morning. We embarked at Antwerp, the chief port of Belgium, and directly on entering the town were confronted by a crowd of barefooted lads, who offered to push our bikes for "von penny." This capital, which has a population of over 232,000, is very picturesqe, and pleased us immensely. Its fine cathedral and churches, in Gothic arthitecture, and its ornate municipal buildings are one mass of artistic carv ing. Like true Britons we went to service at the Cathedrel in the morning. One sermon during the morning was gone through in our language, but the service, of course, was in Latin, seeing that the edifice is a Roman Catholic Church. Whilst there we did not fail to visit the Art Gallery, which con tains Rubena' celebrated masterpieces. But Sunday ended at noon, and so we acted up to the adage "When you are in Rome do as the Romans do." In the afternoon we visited the Vellodrome, a sort of athletic ground. Some sports were in progress, and the entries included several Englishmen. We soon experienced the laxity of the law abroad, as com pared with that of our own country. It happened in this wise. During the sports rain commenced to fall rather heavily, and the promoters decided to postpone the sports. This evidently did not meet with the approval of the crowd, and a scene, which in England would be called a disgraoeful riot, followed. Chairs were first pitched on to the track, then followed forms and anything handy. Finally the barricades were broken down, and the people rushed on to the track to the tent occupied by the judges and journalists. Meanwhile the officers of the law and the well-to-do people stood apart and watched the scene with evident amusement.

What on earth has she left us, 1 ask ye?" "Never mind, father," he said. " Before she can crowd us out of our professions she will have to make the world understand that she is better capable of filling these than we are. If she prefers our dress to her own, 1, for one, have not the slightest objection to her donning it. I don't be lieve she does, however. It is only a passing fancy —a hobby she has got held of through riding the bicycle. She will drop it after a little." "1 dunno 'bout that, Philip, my boy. Did you ever know a woman ter drop anything she'd set her mind 'pan? She hain't dropped medicine, nor the law, nor politics, nor the woman's sutlerin' business, nor nothing 'oepting her womanhood an' her modesty. Don't you be too sartin' she's a goin' ter give up her trousers." But they are not real trousers," objected Philip, "but simply adivided skirt which she wears for convenience sake in riding the bicycle. Look down the street there an' see that gal a-walkin"long side tel her tricycle, an' then tell me them things she's got on don't have the look of genooing trousers furrin ones at that! text: A New Brunswick man named Ryan has invented what he calls a " Merry-Go-Round Ferry." It is believed by Mr Ryan that it will help to solve the problem of rapid transit an large cities, particularly those winch, for example, are divided by • narrow river, wig& must be crossed at many points to accommodate a heavy traffio. The folo . ving description, together with the illustration, gives a very good idea of what the "ferry" is like. In the first place, • substantial pier is erected in the centre of the stream to be crossed. This pier rotate on • stone foundation built up from the bed of the the stream. On top of the pier is a steel track forming • circle round it. On this track rim large rollers A steel platform rests on the rollers and covers the pier. An immense cylinder is at, tached to the centre of the platform, and runs down through the centre of the pier. At the bottom of the cylinder ase ball-bearirgg groves, on which run large steel 'tails. At the top of this cylinder, a few feet below the platform, are other ball-bearings. A tall steel tower, its construction reminding one of the famous Eiffcll Tower in Paris, rain; on the platform. At the base of the tower two great steel arms are connected. These are se.urely attached to a steel cable, which runs to the apex of the tower from either side. An immense steal car is suspended from the end of each arm. These are made in the form of a horseshoe, with the open end facing the wharf or boniing. In the centre of the car is the cabin for foot-passengers, filled with cushioned seats and every convenience necessary for comfort. The platform of this car is large enough, so that horses and carriages, as well as electric cars, may find room on it, using the sides of the car and facing the landing, as the " nierry-g,sround" starts. For conveying electric oars across the stream a trolley wire circles the horseshoe-shaped car. This wire de rives its power from dynamos situated in the pier. Of course the tower , nd its projecting arms, which carry the suspended ors, must move when the Viatform does, and this is simple, because, as already explained, there are ball-bearings and a roller beneath the platform. The elees trio or steam power for operating the revolving structure is concealed within the pier, and connected with the moving platform by cog-wheels. Only one-half of the entire weight of the revolving part rests on the rollers and ball-bearings. This is accomplished by a method which at pre sent Mr Ryan is keeping to himself. At first thought it would seem doubtful if sufficient power could be had to operate such a structure, but Mr Ryan reminds us that the Ferris wheel, and the great see-saw recently devised, with huge stool arm, that carry immense ars loaded with people and elevates them into mid-air, are structures whose weight runs up into hundreds of. tons. The advantages which the inventor of the " Merry-Go-Round Ferry" claims for it over the suspension or drawbridge are threefold. F irst that its construction will consume not more thin one-half the material of the other structures named, thereby costing that much less to build. heooncl a t hat it does away with a large amount of work in repairs. Third, that it it • greet economiser of slake, and that vessels may pass in either ion while it is in motion.

text: A correspondent Writes :—From lapse of time and loss of all authentic record it would be impossible to show what was the original intention of the former inhabitant 4 of Fordington in placing the old stone at the corner of the road facing the Green. text: A wages dispute between some Italian workmen and their employer, a contractor named Wheeler, caused an exciting scene in Philadelphia on Wed nesday night week. About 100 angry Italians sur rounded the Morrisville Hotel, where Wheeler is staying, and remained there all night in order to prevent his escape. They divided themselves into two parties, one of which slept while the other kept watch. Wheeler had a score of his American fore men with him armed to the teeth. He is the con tractor for the construction of a trolley road, and the Italians, who say they have had no money from him for six weeks, that night threatened that if they were not paid they would set the hotel on fire and kill Wheeler. They assert that they subsisted on credit until Saturday, when the tradesmen refused to let them have anything more. Wheeler tried to induce the Italians to return to work on Wednes day, but they drove him to his hotel, at the same time waving revolvers and knives.

text: AMERICAN EXTRAVAGANCE. The one drawback to American hospitality is that it is apt to be tc-o profuse. I have more than once had to offer a mild protest against being et.tertained by a hard-working brother jonnielit on a scale that would hare befitted a millionaire_ The possibility of returning the compliment in kind affords the canny Scot but poor consolation. A dinner three times more lavish and expensive than you want is not sweetened by the thought that you may in turn give your host a dinner three times more expensive and lavish than he wants. Both parties on this system suffer in di gestion and in pocket, while only the hotel-keeper is the gainer. It seems to me, on the whole, that in this country the millionaire is too commonly allowed to fix the standard of expenditure. Society would not be lees, but more, agreeable if, instead of al ways emulating the splendours of Lucußus, people now and then studied the art of Horatian frugality. And I note that in club life, if the plutocrat sets the standard of expenditure, the aristocrat looks to the training of the servants. Their obsequious ness is almost painful. There is not the slightest trace of democratic equality in their dress, their mar.ners, or their speech. Take it all in all, America is a trying place of sojourn for the aforesaid canny §cot,—the man who, without being stingy (oh, dear, no!), has " all his generous impulses under perfect control." The sixpences do not " bang " in this country; they crepitate, they crackle, as though shot from a Maxim quick-firer. For instance, the lowest electric trolley fare is twopence-halfenny. It is true that for five cents you can, if you wish it, ride fifteen or twenty miles; but the advantage becomes inappreciable when, you don't want to ride more than half a mile.

text: AN ADJUNCT TO THE MAIL SERVICE.—The em ployment of trolley cars to assist in distributing the mails has proved quite satisfactory in Brooklyn. The part of the car reserved for the post-office is especially fitted up for this purpose. The equip ments of the travelling post office are similar to those ordinarily used. Several postal clerks accom pany the car, and they open the mail bags and sort and arrange the mail cu the route. The cars stop to take on and let off passengers in the usual way. They are run directly into the post-office yards to load or unload the mails. In this work the trolley lines are looked upon as regular snail routes, and are regularly engaged and paid by Government. AN INTERESTING DISCOVERY.—A house recently unearthed near Pcinpeii is said to be in a more per fect condition than any building yet discovered. It contains several large apartments and three bath rooms, with the basins in sculptured marble, and with leaden pipes ornamented with bronze faucets. The three rooms correspond, says a writer, in descri bing the discovery, to the " calidaritim, epidarium, and frigidarium," which were always to be found in ancient houses of the first class. In consequene of the eruption of Versuvius in A D. 79, the Pompeiian houses brought to light heretofore have been rocfless almost without exception. This one is perfect, and arobreologists are happy over the fact. The roof measures almost 441 t. in length. AN IDEAL MAN.—Here is the winning answer to the question, "What kind of a man does woman most admire?" The man must interest by uncom monness, either in appearance or manner, or he must have that indescribable quality called charm. He must know his own mind and steadily work thereto, even to masterfulness. He disregards "they say," and is not one of a herd. His friends are men, not women. He is only once deceived by the same person. His perhaps hasty temper never runs to unkindness. He needs sympathy and solace in a sometimes divine discontent. He abides under no failure,but goes steadily on. His occasional want of cuccess only attaches and rivets his determination. A GAY CENE.—Ns more brilliant scene can be imagined than a dancing palace in the Isle of Man at what may be called high tide. The floor is immense; four or five thousand young men and women are dancing on it ; the young men in tennis 'flannels and coloured scarves, the young women in light muslins and straw hate. You fed: in the gallery and look down. Sometimes the white lights in the glass roof are covered with red and blue and yellow, and these tints are cast on to the dancers. This simple artifice is astounding in its effects. The mere sense of size and the pre sence of so much life must count fer a great deal. foe have to witness the scene in order to realise its ex tracrdinary fascination. The low buzz of the dancers' feet, the clang and clash of the brass instruments, the boom of the drum, the quake of the great glass house itself, and the low rumble cf the hollow roof beneath—it is like one thing only that I can dreams of or imagine —a battlefield set to music.

text: But steam railways are not immortal. Dike all human vanities they endure but for a season. Already there are signs of a change for some safer and quicker means of transportation, and prophets have arisen who warn us that steam power has nearly reached its culmination, and that the steam locomotive will soon be a thing of the past. Electric locomotives are already in practical use and the electric trolley system is gaining ground where ever it has been tried. We are asiured that the Ameri can Railway Companies are experiencing severe compe tition from this quarter, and their diminishing profits testify to the popularity of the new rival. So great has been the success of " the blithe little trolley" in America that in many of the larger cities it has completely captured the cheap transportation field, and that, too, within a very brief period. That it is mere economical than tramways, the following state ment of the working expenses for a month of tho two systems over The as me track seems to prove. The tram ways employed 450 horses, wihch consumed 94tons of cut hay, about B,ooolbs. feed, and two tons of straw. This, with shoeing cost the company about 4,500 dots. Against this the coal consumed in the same period for electrical maintenance cost 285 dollars, or a clear saving by the trolley of 3,915 dollars. On an average 80 men were employed around the stables and in the car sheds for looking after these 450 horses. For these the com pany substitutes two or three electrical operatives, and saves about 5,000 dollars a month in expenses, besides anticipating a large augmentation of business. The machinery is so purely automatic and so easily manipulated that the material out of which drivers and conductors are made was worked over in a day into ' electric motor-men, who, instead of a wilder, found a far more tractable and manageable horse—one that went without whip, reins, or word of command; one that needed not to be put in or out, or changed for shorter or longer routes. text: By the majority of people doubtless the Rhymney Valley is not considered as a place where poverty lurks, but in the light of the details disclosed of the death of one Georgina Jones, of the Old Woollen Factory, Bargoed, which occur red on Wednesday, the 30th November, it would appear that there are at least some cases of the direst poverty even here. To .recapitulate the case briefly we may say that the deceased and her husband, Mathias Jones, who were somewhat elderly people, had formerly lived at Newbridge, and had only come to Bargoed about five weeks ago and had come to the house above mentioned, which is owned by Mr. and Mrs. Price, of Capel Street, Bargoed. At New bridge, according to Mr. Tom Howe, Mr. and Mrs. Jones had a most comfort able home, and that the deceased's husband had be en a sculptor in a good position and had occasionally attribu ted articles to the Press. Surely things, however, had changed since Mr. and Mrs Jones had come to Bargoed, for their home, which had the appearance more of an outbuilding than a house, pos sessed what may be described as the smallest minimum of furniture, and Mrs. Jones, during her distressing illness, could only be accommodated with what looked like a rough mattress on a low wooden trolley. Accustomed to certain fits during the past four years it was not to be wondered at that under the cir cumstances described the poor woman should again be afflicted, which present attack commenced on the 20th of Nov ember, culminating fatally ten days afterwards, as above stated. During the illness, strange to say, the deceased was not medically attended, although at the last moment a letter was sent to Mrs. Jones' former medical adviser at New bridge, but that communication, which was eventually received by the doctor who had removed to Cardiff, arrived too late to be of service. As no doctor had seen Mrs. Jones before her death the particulars of the case were laid by Police-sergeant Nicholls before the Cor oner for the district, Mr. R. J. Rhys, who conducted an enquiry into the cir cumstances at the Junction Hotel at 3.30 on Friday afternoon last.

text: Capital! the huge god still rides on through the land, and numbers who rejoice in being called men kiss the ground over which its carwheels roll, whilst others, still more infatuated, have thrown themselves in front of it, and have been crushed to powder beneath this modern Jugger naut of civilized and Christianised countries. What infatuation for men who delight to be thought intelligent to thus kiss the rod with which they are whipped, and like the kicked dog, crawl and lick the boots of the brute that kicked it. Capital has been and is now in numerous cases vaunted and trumpeted as the "master" of labour, but though this may be so de facto, it is net so de jure. No such a relation truly exists, but both meet on an equal platform in the present condition of society. If there is any advantage of the one over the other, surely 'tis to labour that the palm must be awarded. When capital is useless and valueless, labour is truly useful and valuable. Of what use is all the accumulated capital of England in the wild woods, or on the wide prairies where, labour cannot be purchased. But labour is far more serviceable under such circumstances, and where our scion of a titled race would perish surrounded by his gold, the honest son of toil, with nerves of steel and muscles of iron, would live alai prosper. Capital is no longer valuable than in proportion as it can pur chase labour, whereas labour is always valuable, and can, under no circumstances, be dispensed with.
