text: Considerable interest was manifested in Slaith waite and Linthwaite on Wednesday whets it became known that the illuminated electric car would traverse the Linthwaite route that night, and probably arrive at the terminus about 8-30. This method of celebrating the King's Coronation has been very popular in the large towns of York shire and Lancashire, and in consequence of the reports given by those who had seen the cars a great crowd turned out to witness the show. Whilst it was a good way down Manchester Road its advent was marked by a bright glowing firma. meat, and when the car came into sight it appeared as one large ball of tire. Gradually it began to take the form and shape of an ordinary tramcar, decorated with myriads of multi-coloured electric lights that shone with dazzling brilliance as it descended the slops towards the terminus. The car contains an aggregate of 1.200 lights of five or six shades of colour. Along the top portion on one side are the words formed by lights " Long live the King," and on the opposite side 'God bless our Queen" At the front of the car was an attractive device forming the letters " E.R." and at the other end a large star that glittered and shimmered with quite magnificent effect. In addition to these features the handrails and trolley arm were covered with rows of various-coloured lights, while flags and bunting completed a novel and thoroughly successful spectacular display. Travelling on the car were the Mayor and Mayoress of lluddersfield, Councillor Moore, chairman of the Tramways Committee; Councillor Oxley, vice chairman; Councillor Cartwright, Alderman Jno. Sugden, Councillor J. Berry, Councillor J. W. Freer, chairman of the Linthwaite Council, Mr. .Thomas, manager; Mr. Hartley, traffic assistant ; Mr. Wilson, electrician, and others. Mr. Joseph Berry called for three cheers for the King, but the response was not a very enthusiastic one. Neither was the attempt to sing "God save the King," attended by a much better result. Either the crowd's coronation enthusiasm had all evaporated, or the magnificent display had bereft them of speech; they neither sung nor shouted, only looked on and looked again. Mr. Berry in vited three cheers for the Mayor and Mayoress, and then the Mayor conferred a similar favour , on the Chairman of the Tramways Committee, and after several people had boarded the car it moved off on its return .jourugy ' and everybody , seemed to consider it " fair gl.d." At Milnsbridge, on the return journey, the brass band poured forth the strains of the National Anthem as the car approached the passing place, and "Rule Britannia" WAS also played. A visit was afterwards paid to Longwood where the car again excited much attention.

text: ELECTRIC TRAMWAYS IN AMERICA. A correspondent forwards some extracts from • &reale in the New York Journal of Commerce on the uses of , electricity, which asserts that as a motive power electricity is winning a most condemnatory record. I This is especially true as to the trolley system, which is preeminently dangerous to life, and I destructive to peace and olmfort wherever it is need. In Newark the accidents average over one a day. In Boston several hundreds are killed or seriously injured every year. In other cities the proportion is equally great. Speaking of Brooklyn, the same paper states that "only a small section of the city has yet been touched by the system, but the casualties make an interesting item in almost every day's issue of the public papers. The killing and maiming, however, have only just begun. Net quite a three-hundredth part of the lines to be propelled by the trolley has yet been changed, 'and if the proportion holds good when all are in operation there will be from a thousand to fifteen hundred persons killed or injured every week throughout the year. text: Evidently the trolley problem has not been solved yet; for there are still plenty of applications at the Patent Office for patents on trolley guards, and the like. But an American inventor his apparently given up the idea that trolley wheels can be made to stick to ,the wire, and has endeavoured instead merely to alleviate the trouble by providing an electric light near the end of the pole to assist the 'conductor in replacing the trolley at night. The electric lamp is lighted by a battery located in the body of the car. A switch is interposed in the circuit near the lamp, and to one end of this switch the trolley rope is attached. Normally this switch is held open by a spring; but when the conductor pulls the rope to draw down and replace the trolley the switch is closed, lighting the lamp, and thereby facili:ating the work of placing the wheel in proper contact with the wire. Connected in series with the tiolley lamp are a number of lamps in the car, which serve to illumine the same while the trolley is being replaced.

text: Experiments were made in Blackpoo last week, with the invention patented by Mr. R. C. Quin, the Borough Electrical Engineer, to minimise the danger of electric wires. The appliance is an ingenious "cut off," which allows of a trolley wire, should it fall, becoming dead, or should telephone wires foul a trolley wire there would be similarly no danger. The experiments were witnessed by several electrical engineers and chairmen of electric committees in other towns. One of the experiments was the cutting of a telephone wire, which caused a slight fizzle as it touched the trolley wire. Immediately, however, the automatic cut-off was brought into operation, and Mr. Quin pulled the wire down with bare hands. Half-a-dozen telephone wires were afterwards dropped across the live trolley wire with the same result. Finally the trolley wire itself was severed, but in every case the " cut-off " acted instantly.

text: Horse-racing by electric light has been tried at St. Louis, U.S., with great success. Th e course at South Side Park presents a curious appearance--the stand, fences, posts, and everything palatable about it being of dazzling whiteness. Upon this, at intervals of twenty-five feet, are strong clusters of incandescent lamps, with four lights in each cluster. Giant search lights illuminate the turns. A peculiar arrange ment prevents the casting of Shadows, whi c h h as always hitherto proved the difficulty in horse-racing by artificial light. The grand stand is a blaze of brilliant whiteness, and from it the course is seen mapped out in a light so bright that the colours of the jockeys' jackets are plainly visible. The effect is all the more intense from contrast with the space of darkness that intervenes between the stand and the track. To obviate danger, only five horses are allowed in each race. The only difficulty ex perienced at the recent meeting was to find sufficient accommodation for the large number of horses entered.

text: How is one to know whether an electric) shock is likely to prove fatal or not? In con sidering the case of a fallen trolley wire carry ing current at a pressure of 500 volts, the severity of the shock will depend altogether, says Mr. Charles R. Gibson in Electricity 01 To-day: its Work and Mysteries Described in Non-Technical Language," upon the resistance offered to the passage of the current from the - 1 wire through the body to earth. The resistance of the body alone will not prevent the current getting through, but if the person is standing on the paved street, and especially if the stones be dry, there is very considerable resistance placed-. in the current's path, and the shock will not be fatal, if it is even severe. Sometimes when an overhead wire has fallen down upon the paved street, the wire has remained "alive," for the path offered the current does not enable suffi cient to rush to earth to operate the safety de vices. A fallen line should never be handled , with the bare hands until one is assured that the line is dead. If it is necessary to handle the line, and rubber gloves are not available. it , should be grasped with a folded newspaper, a cap or - tobacco pouch covering the hand. With these precautioas a live wire can immediately be rendered dead by lifting it into contact with the rails.

Two points about the wires call for notice. One is that they are divided into half-mile sections. Speaking of wires reminds me too that I asked my friend the assistant engineer a very important question. " Suppose - said I, 'the wire breaks at any point and falls on somebody. what, will happen?" text: Important Decision At the Leigh Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. M. F. Burrows (presiding),and other magistrates, the South Lancashire Tramways Company summoned Mr. George Shaw, managing director of .Messrs, G. Shaw and Co., Limited, brewers, Leigh, and four employees of, the firm for obstructing the company's tramcars. Mr. Blair, barrister, appeared for the Tramway Company,and Mr. Sutton, barrister, defended. The first c4se taken was that against Johnson. Johnson, a carter in the employ of the defendant company for obstruction on the 9th inst. 1 Mr. Blair said that on the 9th inst. a tramcar was going down Pennington-bridge, Leigh, in the direction of Lowton,and a brewery cart was coming up the bridge on its left or proper side. The road was too narrow at this point to allow the cart to continue on its own side and pass the tramcar, but the driver of the cart refused to crossover to the other side of the road and allow the tramcar to pass. The result was that the cart and the tramcar stood facing each other twent3 minutes, each refusing to budge, and at the end of that time the tram car driver reversed his trolley and backed to the loop at the top of the bridge. He submitted that the intro duction of the tramways had altered to some extent the question of the rules of the road, and that there had been ol struction. Mr. Sutton, for the defence, submitted that it was a misapprehension to suppose that a tramway conmany lied any right beyond what was given to any ordinary person. The case was disraigsed as were two similar cases. The Bench said they were advised that the Tramways Act did not appear to have altered the law existing prior to the Tramways Act as to the customary rights of the public with respect to highways, consequently the defendants were not acting unlawfully in maintaining their right to make use of their near or customary driving side, and the cases were therefore dismissed. They thought that the question of law should be decided by a higher court. Five guineas costs were allowed in the ,first case, and the *ordinary costs in the other cases.

text: In engineering parlance thev are termed goliatlis. The oharacteristic of the goliath is that a bridge, supported on tall end-framings, carries a crab, or trolley, which picks up and transports the load. In the gantry type there is no bridge, only a jib, from which depends the chain which lifts the weight. Goliaths may be stationary or made to travel up and down the ship-yard on rails. One under notice is a stationary Goliath built by Messrs. Vickers. Sons, and Maxim at their ship yards at Barrow-in-Furness. It is known as a 150- ton crane. but has frequently lifted weights of 175 tons. From the aster level it has a total height of 180 feet. We get an idea of its enormous height. when it is stated that if it were re-erected in Palace Yard, Westminster, it could easily lift up Big Ben, with all its chimes, from the ground rand place it on top of the clock tmver. ! The crane has a total radius of 150 feet, but, as ! will ba readily understood, the lifting power is reduced as the depending chains reach the end of the projecting arm. At a radius of 71 feet the lifting power is 150 tons, the load being gradually reduced to 135'1eet. at which distance the crane can lift 53 tons. The gradual reduction of the weight as the limit of range is reached is neces sary on account of the enormous strain thrown upon structures of this description. The engineer knows at once the weight of the load, this being registered on a special dial in the operator's house on the under side of the lifting jib. The crane is worked entirely by electricity, the mere action of pulling over levers causing the !cad to be lifted clear of the ground, the arm of the crane to swing, in the right direction, and the object carried to be lowered in the desired posi tion.

text: In the Queen's Bench Division, on Friday, Mr. Justice Grantham and a common jury heard an ction by a carman named Durban to recover darnagei from the defendants, Messrs. Hodgman, pleasure van proprietors, of Ramsgate, for injuries to plaintiff's right eye, produced from the "flick" of the whip with which the defendant Arthur Hodgrn in was driving.—The plaintiff's case was that he was driving a trolley from York-street into Queen-street, Ramsgate, at a rate of about five miles an hour, but, hearing the defendant Arthur behind him with a brake and four horses, he pulled up to enable the defendant to pass. In passing defendant struck his horses with the whip, and, in doing so, flicked plaintiff in the eye with the end of the whip, the result being that the eye was so badly injured that plaintiff had to be taken, first to the infirmary at Ramsgate, then to the Royal Ophthalmic Hospital, Westminster, and he was still under medical care.—The defence was that the plaintiff inflicted the injury upon himself, that when told to go higher up with his trolley to enable defendant to pull up opposite a saddler's, plaintiff struck his horse, when the thong caught in the harness or shaft, and in jerking it free the thong struck him in the right eye.—The jury found for the plaintiff, and assessed the damages at £so.—His lordship gave judgment accordingly.

text: Most of our readers will have heard of the revolu tion which is likely soon to take place in the coal trade by the introduction of machinery. There is no doubt that we are on the verge of very great and important changes; and it is highly probable that the old system of hewing will be superseded, and the miner will consequently be relieved from a great amount of manual labour. We have the pleasure now to call attention to a machine invented by Mr. Thomas Harrison, engineer, of Tadhoe Ironworks, which is unsurpassed for its simplicity of construc tion and its general efficiency—not the least notice able features being the exceedingly low price at which it can be supplied, and the economy attending its working, the small coal being about one-third the quantity made by the usual process of working. This machine is on the revolver cutter principle, driven by a turbine, which is made to rotate by means of compressed air, at a pressure of from 15 to 20 lbs. per inch, and performs about 600 revolu tions per minute. The construction of the machine is, as nearly as we are able to describe, as follows: —The cutter-wheel is mounted en a transverse slide, which is placed upon a frame, trolley, or car riage; and the transverse slide is arranged so as to allow of the cutter-wheel being placed under or above, to afford such facilities for working as the peculiar circumstances of the seam may require. The turbine is carried on a bracket resting on the centre pin of the cutter-wheel. The air is con veyed into the top of the turbine from a receiver or blast-pipe, and may be connected with ordinary hose-piping. The current of air rushes through the turbine at a velocity equal w 1,700 feet per second, and is supplied at the rats of 240 cubic feet per minute. Such a quantity of air rushing into the confined workings of a coal mine must be of considerable service in ventilating the pit. The cutters, which are six in number, may be arranged so as to cut any distance from the "thin," and to any required depth, from 12 inches to 3 feet. This wheel, into which the cutters are fixed, is propelled to its work by a scroll and scroll wheel conveniently situated on the back of the carriage; und the trans verse slide which carries the cutter wheel is moved backwards or forwards, to or from the coal, at pleasure by a quick pitched screw placed underneath the slide. We understand that the estimated capa bilities of this very admirable invention is 400 tons per day. During the last two weeks a series of trials have taken place at Tadhoe, which have convinced those who are best able to judge of the superiority of this cutter over any which has hitherto been brought before the public. Among the gentlemen who have seen the machine tried are Black the following : —W. R. Atkinson, Esq., her Majesty's Inspector of Mines; Richard Johnson, Esq., of lini WaLamscish.wjinW.ealLnol:o's—dE;sclaEa.n'tsqh'o.efE, f rsßack Boy Coal Co. ; J Greener s ' Esq., of South Hatton; W m of agents to C o l one l S to b art ; Coxhoe ; and Willi am A rm . strong, told, ongiE Esq., of Wingate G range, a l l of whom, we a press their unqualified approval of the machine. The one we had the pleasure of seeing has been purchased by the owners of the Hetton collieries, and will shortly be subjected to another test. It is to be tried and compared with Ridley's famous patent, and we are assured that the inventor and patentee of this machine has no misgivings as to the result.

text: Mr. Preece, C. 8., the electrician to the Post Office— surely a practical expert if there ever was one—has re cently enumerated some instances of the development of electricity that would seem incredible did they come from a less authoritative source. Mr.Preece tells us that, having demonstrated over and over again the possibi lity of sending messages through some miles of wireless space, he at length has been able to put his discoveries to a practical test. "A few days ago," he says, " the cable which runs from Oban to the Island of Mull got out of order. Connection by induction was effected across the Sound of Mull at the narrowest part,which is about two miles wide." A person now signing a cheque, say in Paris, can have the signature simultaneously re produced in London. To watch the movements of a pen guided by an invisible hand, as the writer recently did, is calculated to make even a strong-nerved person ex tremely uncomfortable. When the merits of that extremely sensitive instru ment the thermopole come to be more generally recog nised, the doctors at a fever hospital sitting in their offices will receive instant intelligence of any rise in the temperature of patients. The thermopole was used when Sir W. Harcourt's son was lying ill with typhoid at the Treasury. One night the temperature nearly reached 105 degrees. The watchful little instrument instantly flashed the rise through the wire to the doctor's house, arousing the sleeper,who was in his patient's room with in half-an-hour. It will probably sound fantastic, if not absurd,to talk about the odours of sweet-smelling flowers being electri cally transmitted, but the statement is made in all sober earnes'ness. The competition of the electric trolley lines has brought down the fares on the Philadelphia and Reading, and is expected to do so on the Penn sylvania Railway. And, finally, the greatest project of all, the Inter-Oceanic Electric Railway, has been incor porated in Illinois with a capital of 200,000,000d015. American engineers seem to be all agreed that steam railwaya are doomed within a quarter of a cen tury, so far as America is concerned.

text: Much interest is taken in electricity just now as a motive power. In America it is applied in many towns to the tram systems. The city of Bristol, where electrical traction has been applied to tramways, lies in a kind of basin, with hills all round to which the suburbs have extended. Only a few of these districts, where the rcads are for the most part less steep, are served with tram ways worked by horse power. The road is constructed of heavy steel girder rails, upon a bed of con crete, double lines being placed in the wide thoroughfares and a single line in the narrow ones. In order to ensure a perfect connection between every rail for the electrical current to pass along them, they are united by copper bonds or pieces of thick copper wire. Ornamental standards or posts of steel, bearing brackets ex tending over the roadway and carrying continu ous wires, are constructed at short intervals along the route In the broad thoroughfares these posts are placed between the up and down lines with an arm stretching out on either side, but in the narrow streets they stand beside the road and carry one arm. The station where the electrical power is generated is situated mid-way between the two termini, and the motive force is sent out from powerful dynamos along a cable laid under ground, from which the electricity is conveyed to the overhead wires up the posts at intervals of half a mile. Further, "taking into consideration the two prime factors, namely, the number of those employed, and the regularity of those employed, machinery does not favour the in creased steady demand for labour." I have nothing to say against the use of maohinery, nor against mother nature giving out her secrets at the call of the scientist. Nor yet would I bottle up the inventive faculty. text: Nsanow ESCAPE.—Lord Coventry's hunting party met with a mishap on Wednesday, which narrowly escaped resulting in serious consequences. When hunting in the West of Warwickshire his lordship has been in the habit of bringing his men and horses and hounds by train to Aloester Station; but on Wednesday the party alighted at Conghton Station, about a mile and a half from Alcester, where the meet was announced. Three horse-boxes and a private carriage concained the party, and no sooner had these been detached from the ordinary train which brought them than they began to run backwards in the direction of Alcester. His lord ship and others had left the train before the car riages were detached, but two of the whips and a groom, with the horses and hounds, remained in the horse-boxes, which rapidly gained momentum. Fortunately, the runaway carriages were noticed as they approached Alcester, and a man, named John Cornwall, had the presence of mind to turn them into a siding, where their force were broken before coming to a dead-stand by a platelayer's trolley, and the men and horses escaped with a severe shaking. Had the carriages not thus been intercepted they must have gone some miles down the line in the direction of Evesham, there being a gradient the whole of the way, and a goods train being due in the opposite direction, the consequences must have been very serious.

text: On Wednesday evening week a earn of upwardl. 4 of £lOO was publicly presented to Thomas Sher rock, of 21, Chatsworth-street, Rose Hill, Wigan, who, although blind from birth, has worked over thirty years in coal mines in the Pemberton dis trict. There was a large attendance of prominent gentlemen of the township of Pemberton, and the career of Sharrock, as related by the various speakers. was certainly of a most extraordinary character. The recipient made a statement, iii which. he said he was about 54 years of age, and from birth had been afflicted with cataract, which produced blindness. A brother and sister were afflicted. When quite young he began working iii the galleries, drawing for six men, who were en gaged coaling, and he also acted as hooker.on. It was whilst employed at this particular mine that he sustained the only injury ho had experienced in the whole of his colliery life, and that injury was con fined to a slight wrench caused in lifting a trolley on to the rails. After working there three or four years he went to draw at the Nerley Collieries, and had to travel over 600 yards to the working place, whilst later he was employed at the Walthew House Pit. At that pit, Sharrock stated, there were seven blind men all working in one shunt as "putters." Singular to say, it was his duty to commence all new men, and he had to take them to their work ing places. Wnen lights were out ha used to lead the colliers out of their working places or take their lamps to the lamp station at the pt bottom to get them relighted. He knew every inch of the airways and travelling roads, and could get from one place to another quite as easily as he could move about at home. Subsequently he was engaged as a drawer at Blundell's Collieries, and after 21 years' service in those mines he had just retired. text: Progress of the Work. • The construction and erection of this inaportsnt and interesting work has been well advanced during the last six months, and although considerable progress has been made on the site, still more has been made at the con tractor' works. Oa the Runcorn side, a large amount of masonry and earthwork to form the new road approach has been completed, and most of the large cast iron cylinders which form the base of the towers have been sunk to the level of the rock, about 25 feet below the bed of the Manchester Ship Canal. As some of our readers may possibly not know the nature of the work which is being carried out, the fol lowing brief description may be of interest :—The pre sent accommodation for wheel traffic between Widnes and Rancern is either by Warrington Bridge or by the cumbersome ferry boats at Liverpool ; and foot passen gers have to pay twopence, climb an incline at the I Widnes side, walk across the London and North-Western I Railway bridge and then descend by a long flight of I steep steps into Runcorn. TbP bridge under course of construction will do away with this uncomfortable unsatisfactory and expensive means of transit ; and passengers end all kinds of traffic will be conveyed across the river and Ship Canal under three minutee at the small charge of one penny for passengers and a varying charge for vehicles according to the nature of the goods and size of the vehicle. The bridge itself is really a suspension bridge without the usual approaches at each end ; which are costly in construction and in the purchase of the necessary lands and buildings. At each end of the bridge are two steel towers about 175 feet high ; these towers support the cables—which are about 12 inches diameter—from which are suspended two stiffening girders nearly 30 feet in depth. Upon the outer bottom flange of these girders are fixed ordinary rails upon which run a trolley 70 feet long, from which is suspended a car. This car will be about twelve Ifeet clear of high water spring tides, and will run from one side of the river to the other. It will be driven by electric niotors and will be capable of carry ing at one time four two-home farmers' waggons (laden), and 300 passengers, and will make the passage from cue side of the river to the other in 21 minutes. The span between the towers is exactly 1,000 feet ; so the bridge will have the longest span of any bridge carrying wheel and passenger traffic in the United King dom, and is only exceeded in span abroad, by the East River Bridge at New York. It will be nearly twice the span of :,he Menai Suspension Bridge. The t mars at each end rest on eight cast iron cylinders nine feet in diameter ; these are filled with cement and concrete and securely bolted to the rock. The approach to the towers on the Widnes side is by a short length of new road at the bottom of Mersey-road,and thence by a steel viaduct consisting of curved arched ribs of about 55 feet span ; I a similar construction is adopted on the Runcorn side, but the steel arched girders are sborter and the new road of masonry and earthwork much longer. COLOUR OF THE SEA.—The water of the ocean is varied by impurities, and by the colouring effects of the enormous multitudes of various forms of organised life, which sometimes mask the natural colour of the surface of the sea and tinge extensive areas with remarkable colours. Red appears to be most frequently met with. In the southern parts of the Red Sea and in the Arabian Gulf large areas are coloured blood - red by microscopic animaloulte,.and in the Indian Ocean similar forms of life cause, in addition to red, milk-white or yel low spots of great extent, the appearance of which is frequently alarming to the ignorant sailor. Off the Guinea coast ships sometimes appear to float in milk. Extensive red streaks are also known to occur in the South Atlantic and South Pacific, which are caused by hosts of small red crustacea. The " Sea"million of California owes its brilliant colour to infusoria. Areas coloured green have been noted, especially in the Arctic regions which are due to myriads of diatoms, and in some portions of the Antarctic seas diatoms of rusty colour make the water a dirty brown. text: THE AIRSHIP OF THE FUTURE. —An interesting article on terial navigation appears in " McClure s 3lngazine " from the pen of Professor Bell. The professor holds some rather original views on the subject. He maintains that the discovery of the balloen retarded the solution of the flying problem for a century. In his opinion, the fundamental principle of terial navigation is that the airship should be heavier than the air. He says: " Elec tticity in one form or another will undoubtedly be the motive power for airships, and every advance in electrical knowledge brings us one step nearer to the day when we shall fly. It would be perfectly possible to-day to direct a flying machine by means of pendant electric wires which would transmit the necessary current without increasing the load to be carried." As a feasible means of propelling an air ship a kind of trolley system is suggested, the rod hanging down from the car to the wire instead of extending upward. The first witness was Thomas William Traverse, sur veyor, 'Leigh, who produced a plan of the Ship Canal cuttiug at Rixton.--Joieph Arstall, a boot and shoe maker at Rixton, deposed that the deceased man was about 88 years of age, and was an engine driveror tenter, and worked at what was known as the "Rocker" pump. On the morning of Sunday, 27th April, deceased, who lodged at his house, left to go to his work, and witness arranged to take his dinner. On the body being removed to his house and stripped witness saw a small hole in his breast. In reply to Mr. Browne witness said the deceased was a much taller man than the prisoner.—Frank Harris, described as a " slasher " over the engines, and living at the huts, Rixton, said on the Sunday forenoon in question he saw the deceased in the sheds at the canal works and he saw the prisoner near the pumping engine. At the outset it may be stated that the more the matter is considered in the light of expert opinion the more difficult it is to account for the fatal results of the mishap. With the fuller light that will doubtless be thrown upon the matter at the official inquires, causes at present publicly unknown may be traced. The central factor in the matter is that the Liver pool trains are worked by electricity at a pressure of 500 volts, and that pressure is not held to be dangerous. Why the passage of a current at that pressure through the bodies of men and horses should cause death, or whether there was at the time a current of a higher pressure flowing over the conductors, are questions that have yet to be determined. The matter is one of great interest for Bradford, inasmuch as the Bra iford system of municipal trams is practically identical with that on which the accident occurred at Liverpool. Both are on the overhead trolley wire system, and the currents in both places are at a tension of 500 volts. Both places are also subject to the same Board of Trade restrictions with reference to guard wires or shields. Wherever a trolley wire is crossed by a telegraph or telephone wire it must be protected by a guard wire or a wooden shield. The guard wires are stretched above the thick copper conductors along which the trolley runs, and the wooden shields (in Bradford bamboo is used) are fixed to the upper side of the trolley wires. The object of both forms of guard is to prevent a broken telegraph or telephone wire which falls across the road from coming into actual contact with the trolley wire, along which the 500 volt current is flowing. If a telephone or telegraph wire did come into contact in this way, the delicate instruments with which it was connected would be ruined, or, at the best, "cut out" by the burning of the safety fuses which protect them. This, of course, is quite apart from any questions of possible injury to human beings. All these precautionary measures are carefully inspected by Board of Trade officials before the line can be used. At Liverpool it appears to be clear that the fallen telephone wires did touch the trolley wires, and thus conducted the current to the persons in the street who were killed or injured. text: The cable supplying the current to the electric cars at Haslingden fell on Tuesday night about eleven o'clock for a distance of nearly half a mile —from the Commercial Hotel to Bank Mill-street. It is believed from investigation that a car trolley pole caught one of the fastening ears near the bot tom of Princess-street, that this liberated the wire from the ear, and that the weight of the wire caused it to tear the wire away from the other ears within the distance stated. The recent frost and snow would probably assist the collapse. When the wire touched the ground a brilliant blue flash was given out, the effect being similar to the dis charge of a weak flash of lightning in the imme diate vicinity. Very fortunately the portion of the track affected was at the time clear of persons and of vehicular traffic, or the results would have been serious. Several persons had, however, crossed this portion of the track less than a minute before the collapse. The occurrence caused great alarm to a few people who were near the Commer cial Hotel, 801110 of whom screamed. The occur rence incidentally led to the paying of a strong tribute to the cable fastening patented by Mr. Barnes Kay, the Haslingden tramway manager, which avoids the use of solder and substitutes a grip by tongueing and grooving. In every case , where the cable catne from the ears it had been attached by soldering. At each end—Bank Mill street and the Comniercial—the collapse was elE•cked when the falling wire came to one of Mr. Kay's fastenings, although the strain on the ear at Bank Mill-street was so severe that the weight of the wire bent the carrying arm. text: The plaintiff in this action was Josiah Yeoin . a . ris Robins, West Hill, Cubbington, gentleman. and the defendants were the Great Western Lai w.i Company, Paddington. Heath. solicitor, Warwick, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Crowther Davies for the Rail way Company. A plan of the scene of the collision was put in by Mr. Trepess and not disputed by Mr. Davies.—Oeorge Lowe, groom, in the employ of the plaintiff, stated that on the 31st October last lie was driving a pony carriage down Redford Stye( t, Lea ttt ill gton, and turned into Portland Road, where he saw a rail. way van about :10 yards away, in the centre of the road. Witness shouted to the driver to stop, but instead of t:o og so he pulled across the street, and witness was pressed against the pave ment on his right side. The wheel if the van caught. the wheel of the carriage and the hors.. started off. The carriage was pushed back into Redford Street, the pony fell and the carriage was smashed. —Cross-examined by Mr. Davies, witness said ' when he came down Bedford Street lie was driving slowly. The pony wanted to trot, but he would not allow him, and went gently round the corner. The man with the van failed to pull out of the road and consequently ran into the carriage. It was not true that witness came round the corner of the street at a trot on his wrong side, or that in consequence of a hand cart he ran into the trolley. The pony's hock was cut, in consequence of the van having pulled him down.—Thomas Benison, carriage builder, Bedford Street, Leamington, spoke to having been present directly after the accident, and he saw- the carriage had dragged on the i south side. Witness repaired the carriage, and the cost was £5 10s. 6d. Crsss-examined, witness said the groom also came to him and pointed out the damage. The marks on the kerbing on the north side were very distinct.—This was the case for the plaintiff, and the defence was that the accident was brought about by the wilful neg ligence of the plaintiff's groom.—Henry Minchin, carter, in the employ of Harding and Co., stated that on the day in question he was driving a trol ley Mona Portland Road. The horse was walking slowly. 'Witness was on the near side of the road, and on the south side there was a truck standing. Plaintiff's carriage came round the corner at a trot. When the groom of the plaintiff found he could not get through, he backed the trap against witness's near aide, and that started the horse in the van. If there had been no truck in the way there would have been no collision. —Samuel Dingley, waggoner, in the employ of Pickford and Co., corroborated the statement respecting the handcart, which was standing in the street when the accident occurred. He saw the handcart and trolley together, and th,..n he heard the crash.— George Hawtin, porter, Leamington, who was in Bedford Street when the accident occurred, swore that the plaintiff's groom went round the corner at a trot and pulled into Minchin.—His Honour, after visiting and inspecting the scene of the acci dent, dismissed the action.

text: The second annual horse show and parade was held at Neath on Tuesday, under the presidency of the Mayor (Mr J. D. Llewellyn), in truly summer weather: - The parade, which comprised horses and vehicles of all descriptions, was quite a mile in length. Of the working representatives the most noteworthy were those of Messrs Lancaster, Spier, and Co., of a colliery. Mr Temple Stroud (manager) displayed great ingenuity and knowledge in these exhibits. On the first trolley was a repre sentation of a blacksmith's shop and a display of all the appliances used in the winning of coal. Lamps, bores, blasting tools, and surveyors' implements were all included, and the ambulance department was not overlooked. On the next trolley was a realistic vein of coal, with a very real collier working upon it. The mode of timbering was here clearly illustrated. This exhibit included a tram of coal from the colliery managed by Mr Temple Stroud. The parade was an excellent one in every respect. The element of fun was fully supplied by the cyclists in fancy costume. Ally ..sloper," The Jay," The Spanish Muleteer,' and The Baker,' were decided successes. The judging in the ring at the Corporation Field occupied several hours. The attendance was satisfactory, although the recent Swansea Agricultural Show doubtless diminished the number of those who passed the turnstiles. The following were the judges :—Mr J. B. Wayman, Bridgend ; Mr Rees Williams, Llys wen House, Brecon; Mr W. Marsh. Llanelly ; and Mr J. G. Gibbs, Hodgeston. Mr T. M. Curtis, town clerk, was hon treasurer. Mr George T. Sims proved, as usual, an energetic and efficient hon secretary. Mr. George Foster Peabody, of Brooklyn, N.V.,has dispensed with coal entirely,and all house hold operations are now performed by electricity. The house is lighted by electricity, warmed by elec tric heaters and cooled in summer by electric fans ; the cooking is done and all water heated by electri city, and the work of ironing is 'rendered easy by the use of electric irsns, no longer "sad." Whenever power is needed,electric motors are employed,as for running a sewing machine or in laundry operations. Electric traction is proceeding here at a great rate. "Networks" of electric lines are being every where projected. Of long distance line's, that bet ween Chicago and St. Louis seems to be assured of final success. In Pennsylvania and Ohio there are several lines of over 100 miles in length, that are expected soon to be started, and each week the pro jects appear to become bolder. As to street railways, it has been impossible for the large companies,even with their facilities increased to the utmost,to any where nearly equal the enormous demand for the necessary electrical apparatus. Twelve months ago one machine.of which I had charge,turning out five miles of trolley wire a day, was found sufficient.. Now, there are two, with prospects of more,turning out 20 miles a day, improved machinery turning Out more work, but bringinzno more pay. Turning from copper there is bronze, and alumi num. These are metals now drawn as ordinary iron wire. The aluminum business is a rapidly growing one. The metal is a singularly light one, so 'much so that it can be used for all kinds of art and decoration purposes. It can be put to good solid purpose also. Aluminum horseshoes have been tried with remarkably successful results, it is said, by the Russian government. As an experiment a few horses of the Finland Dragoons were shod with one aluminum shoe and three iron shoes each. The result showed that the aluminum shoes preserved the foot better than the iron ones. None of the aluminum shoes broke and they were used over again for reshoeing. Horses are now shod with this metal at a cost of £2—the set. All the aluminum now being made is made by electrical processes. At present its cost is about 2s. per pound. It is ex pected in the near future to be down to Is. per lb. An aluminum and a copper rod of the same size would cost nearly the same. The production in the States is about 150 tons a year. The Metal Reduc tion Co. of Patricroft, Lancashire, produces over 300 lbs. daily. It is also produced at Stoke-on- Trent. I merely make, as it were, passing reference to these matters in the hope of drawing workers' attention to what is going on around us. I don't agitate for eight hours day. I know that the time is near, when the less hours will be.forced upon us. Only workmen must devote their spare time more to study than they have done, or woe betide them. Turning to the June N. A. Orleans, Richmond,- Boston or Philadelphia cheaper than the same articles can from Pennsylvania, Ohio, Tennessee or Alabama. Turn now, in the same number, to Mr. If allocles article on "Who are the wealth producers." He says :—ln the U.S.the same number of men who in the year 1810 produced wealth to the value of a thousand million dollars a year produce at the present day wealth, to the value of two thousand three hundred millions. This increase he rightly ascribes to scientific invention and discovery, and i - nproyed methods of dividing and improving labour.

The 6.10 p.m. train from Bournemouth, consisting of four carriages, a gourd's van, and one of the tindland's engines, had proceeded on its journey towards Bath all right, but, when within about a mile from the Wincanton station, from some unknown cause ' the whole train left the line, and proceeded about 150 yards when the engine turned completely round and fell' over on its back, the carriages being thrown on the opposite side of the line. The guard's van was smashed to pieces, the carriages were also smashed, and the funnel of the engine, which was buried about a foot-and-a-half in the earth, was completely broken off. Assistance was at once procured from Wincanton, and the injured attended to, Dr. Heginbothom, of Bruton, surgeon, who was among the passengers— which numbered over 50—rendering all the help he could. The driver, Thomas Norman, one of the oldest drivers in the company's employ, and the stoker, James Creek, were found in the driving box very badly injured;' especially the former, who was fright fully scalded about the arms and legs and had a very severe cut on the head. With some little difficulty they were extricated and placed on a trolley with Mr, and Mrs. Bishop, of Glastonbury, the latter of whom was very seriously injured, her collar-bone being broken, and Mies Loader, of Wincanton, who was also very much knocked about and had fainted, and were conveyed to the Wincanton Station, from whence they were taken, with the exception of the latter, to the Greyhound Hotel, shereMsens. Mr. BERNAL called attention to the recent accidents on rail ways, and contended that where parties were deriving large profits from them, the public had a right to expect that every attention should be devoted to the safety of those who travelled by them. Sir G. CLERK stated the steps taken by the Board of Trade in all such cases; and after a short discussion, Sir R. PEEL, amidst repeated cheers, said that the railway directors were bound to protect the public. It was no answer, when accidents occurred, to say that in coach travelling accidents were more frequent—they should seek to have no accidents at all. If railway proprietors failed in making proper provision for the safety of the public, he was satisfied that Parliament would not hesitate to diminish their profits, with a view to provide more efficaciously (hr the security of the lives of those whom they con veyed. STATE OF THE NATIONAL DEFENCES. Lord PALMERSTON stated some circumstances of mis management on the Dover line which had come under his own observation; after which, he called attention to the state of our national defences. It was true, he said, that we were on the best terms with France, but it was to be recollected, nevertheless, that France had an army of 360,000 men—a large naval force, parti cularly in war steamers—that a steam bridge might be thrown across the Channel without any difficulty should the present good understanding unhappily be broken, which it might be any month in the year, and that in such an event we were powerless for re sistance. text: .A fearful railway accident occurred on Monday at midnight between Radstock and Wellow, on the Bath and Evercreech branch of the Somerset and Dorset Railway. The line is a single one worked jointly by the Midland and London and South-Western on the absolute block system. An excursion train from Bournemouth to Bath arrived at Righted in safety. It then proceeded onwards to Bath, but waa stopped at the Foxcote Colliery siding, a mil. below Radstock. After a halt of a few minutes th e train proceeded towards Bath, but bad only run a couple of hundred yards when a special train from Bath to Radstock came round a sharp curve, and the two engines, which weighed fifty tons eath, dashed into each other with great loleßce. The men in charge of the Bournemouth Mani escaped, but a large number were injused. more or less seriously. The Radstock train, the speed of which was much Venter, was not so fortunate. Its.grm three carriages were thrown one upon the other, and the passengers, almost without one exception, killed. The first was the van, in which a guard named Wells was travelling. Ile was killed on the Opel, and the next was a third-class coach, in which most of the passengers were travelling, and then fol lowed a composite first .and second-clam carriage. The latter was swung round and pitched upon the embankment, the few passengers St contained escap ing with injuries. The middle carriage of the three dashed into the one before it; both were broken to pieces, and the passengers were mixed up with the wreckage in such a way as to render it impossible to discern in which of the coaches they had been travel ling. A man named Godfrey, who like most of the fourteen passengers killed, was returning to Bed stock from the Bath Regatta, was imprisoned between the engine buffers and the guard's van for three hours. He was sensible nearly all the while, but shortly after he was extricated he died. The colliery officials and Dr. Worger and other local medical men came up; the wounded were attended to and removed to the Both Hospital or to the adjacent houses, and the work of extricating the killed was carried on with all possible vigour by a large body of men sent by the company. This work, however, was a tedious one, as the dibria were interlocked. If rough measures had been resorted to the unfortunate dead would have been still more mangled than they were from the results of the collision. Large fires were lit with the fragments of carriages on the vegetable gardens skirting the line, and the labour was ur gently pursued under the direction of Mr. Dyfonl, superintendent of the tine; Mr. Fisher, locomotive superintendent; Mr. Radway, of Bath, and other officials. It was nearly 12 hours after the accident occurred before the whole of the dead were extricated. In its general aspect the 1900 volume is much like its predecessors, al though, necessarily, by reason of the im mense developments in trading concerns, and the rapid growth of suburban districts, on I a vastly greater scale. When the Directory was first issued in 1760 by Mr. John Gore, it was a sixpenny tract-like small octavo, with single 'column pages. The whole population of the town at that time was only about 25,000, and, of course, all these were not included. 13y the close of the eighteenth century there iad been a considerable development of the people, who numbered at the 1801 census 55,732, while the shipping of the port was 459,719 tons, or about double what it was when the Directory was first issued. Mean while this Directory had also greatly in creased. It had become a quarto of some 90 , pages, about 70 two-column pages of which , are devoted to the list of names and ad dresses. text: A special Berne excursion train which was run into by the Paris express at Zollikofen on Monday morn ingivith fatal effect was partially composed of luggage waggons fitted up with temporary seats and benches for the accommodation of the holiday makers, who were flocking in thousands to take part in the Berne celebrations. The pressure upon all the railway lines had for some days past been very great, and the traffic had been congested to an almost unprecedented degree. When the densely packed local excursion train reached Zollikofen shortly after seven o'clock in the morning it was brought to a standstill, the line being blocked by several other excursion trains in advance. The danger signal still barred its further progress when the Paris express, to which yet another excursion I train from Delamont had been coupled, came up at full speed. As there is a sudden curve in the line at the spot the driver of the express was unable to see the train in front, and his engine dashed with terrible force into the rearmost waggons of the stationary special. The passengers in the latter heard the express approaching, and the few moments' grace they thus obtained were utilised to push the women and children to the doors, the men jump ing out after them. In this way many lives were saved; indeed, all the occupants of the goods wag gons, which had been converted into temporary passenger vans, appeared to have escaped. It was the occupants of the next two ordinary passenger carriages who suffered most. Both coaches were wrecked, and according to the latest information 14 persons, mostly women, were killed on the spot, while at least :14 were seriously injured. The spectacle presented by the dead and wounded, most of whom were in holiday attire, was a most gruesome one, and afforded a revolting contrast to the festivities in which the ill-fated passengers had hoped to participate. The injured were conveyed with all noseible speed to the hospital, and steps were at Once taken by the authorities to bring the popular rejoicings on which the whole town was en gaged to a close at the earliest possible moment. The historical procession which had been organised was in course of formation before the news of the disaster arrived, but all the festivities which had been arranged for the afternoon were abandoned. Those who lost their lives by the accident were all Swiss country people. None of the passengers in the Paris express sustained any serious injury.

text: ACCIDENT ON THE Loot. Ltra.---On Wednesday morning, between breakfast and dinner time, two men named Jolm Towey and Martin Ragan, navvies, met with an accident that might have had very serious results, through the firing of a shot to re move the earth in the cutting near the Cobridge Schoolhouse, where the station for Cobridge is to be built. Towey after charging the shot carelessly went underneath the charge, in the waggon road where all the dirt was expected to fall in the waggons; and Ragan went to talk to him. The firing of the shot threw a large quantity of dirt over Ragan and covered him for more than five minutes, while Towey was cut about the head and by the side of the ear. The debris was removed from Ragan as soon as possible, and Messrs. Hard man and Taylor, surgeons were sent for, the men being attended to immediately. Neither of them are very seriously hurt, and on Thursday were expected to be at work again in a few days. text: AMERICAN RAILWAY ROBBERS. THE LATE ATTACK ON THZ KANSAS EMPRESS. A oorrespondent of the Times at Chicago obtained in formation from a gentleman of that town, who was a passenger, of the robbery of the Kans as express. 1:c says: The affair seems to have been the work of a moment. The train was proceeding smoothly; no one dreamed of insecurity; the passengers were lounging about the cars, and the officials of the train were either asleep or conversing one with another. Suddenly the train stopped, obstructions having been laid on the track, and gun shots and the,sharp crack of the revolver were heard. At the same moment a dozen armed ruffians presented themselves in the coaches. Pointing their rifles, they called upon the astonished pas sengers to surrender. To this admonition the travellers submitted by holding up their hands. Six of the brigands then proceeded to relieve the passengers of their money, watches, and trinkets; while the remainder of the gang were murdering the express officer in their efforts to induce him to open his treasury chest. The engineer and fireman were forced at the point of the rifle to break open the office, their movements being accelerated by the firing of revolvers at their ears. Alto gether the brigands secured between 515,000 and 520,000, as well as a sackful of watches and trinkets. They then decamped, signalising their departure by a fusillade of shots; to use the language of the Chicago gentleman "They skipped op the embankment and were out of sight in a twinkling." Before taking their departure the gang imparted an ante-climax to the drama by distributing rewards to the fireman and engineer for their assistance in breaking open the express officer's car. The unfortu nate officer himself they belaboured in the most brutal manner, by striking him upon the bead and face with their revolvers. The marauders, according to my informant, were all young men; they wore masks, but these were of the flimsiest description; it was easy to discern their features. They were dressed in the approved fashion in the West — that is to say, they wore coloured shirts and dingy blue cotton trousers stuffed into jack boots. Upon their heads were the customary wide-awake hats, and in their belts they each carried a 14-shooter and a bowie knife, their equipment being completed by a Henry rifle. These men are all " dead shots," and their desperation and utter disregard of human life render them a source of terror wherever they appear. The gang which "cluck up . the Missouri express are believed to be well known, and their ultimate captors may be looked upon with certainty. Jesse James, whose name was incidentally mentioned by a member of the band, is known as onset the most despe rate ruffians in the country. He formerly belonged to the gong which owed allegiance to Quentrell, the leader of the troop which figured so ingloriously in the Civil War, and which dyed its name in ineffaceable ignominy by the massacre at Lawrence, in Kansas. Jesse James, how ever, is not now upon the war path in the Kansas terri tory, bet he is believed to be residing upon the residuary gains of his exploits in Texas. The leader of the attack upon the Chicago and Alton train is believed to be iden tical with the leader of the gang which on July 17th stopped and robbed the Chicago and Rock Island express

text: As the present remarkably long continuance of frosty weather is exciting the attention of and becoming a sub ject of serious interes to all classes, it appears that it would not be out of place to put upon record, in a brief way, some account of the remarkable winters that bare visited this country in times lonz gone by as well as in the memory of man. In the reign of Queen Elizabeth, we are told by the noteworthy Hollinshead, that on the 21st day of Decem ber, 1565, there commenced a frost so severe that the river Thames, on New-year's eve, was firmly frozen over, and that people went along and across it as if it had been a high road all the way between London bridge and Westminster. The old chronicler states that games of football were played by the common people on the river, and that the court went upon it and shot at targets. On the 31st January the thaw set in so suddenly that great damage was done, not only on the banks of the river 1 harnea, but on all the rivers throughout the kingdom. Hollinshead mentions that the Ouse Bridge at York was swept away entirely. ' In 1663 there mass very remarkable frost, which began in December, and continued until the 6th of February. On this occasion all the rivers in the country were bound I up. On the Thames there was a fair held and booths erected. A passage was made from the Temple to South wark, along which people were conveyed on horseback. There were shows exhibited, with feats of tumbling and horsemanship, besides bull baiting, and other sorts of amusements of the same kind, so dear to the people of the 'good old times.' On the 2d of February an on was roasted whole at Whitehall, of which Charles II and his Queen partook. This frost broke up so suddenly that the river, which was strong enough to bears coach and six horses in the morning, was at nightso broken up and free of ice as to allow a boat to pass front bank to bank in open water. text: At four o'clock on the morning of November 8th,1875, an express train on the Lehigh Valley Railway in America, was on the top of a mountain, eighteen miles above the city of Wilkosbarre. Among the passengers were the President of the United States and several members of his Cabinet, in a special coach. From this point the grade was very steep, and the road full of curves. It was the custom to keep the brakes sat all the way down. If they failed, disaster was sure to follow. Within a minute after the train started, the driver noticed that something had suddenly gone wrong with the brakes. The train .kept pushing the engine. He reversed,but without checking the speed. Seeing this, the guard and one or two other train men jumped, and escaped with only slight injuries. The train now ran faster and faster, and a horrible death seemed wait ing for all on board. The driver blew the whistle con tinuously to warn trains at the foot of the mountain of his alproach. -When ,the runaway passed Nescopeck station it was goingst rate of nearly seventy miles an hour, and the faithful driveretood at his post,bareheaded holding on, and still blowing the •whistle. At the foot of the mountain all the trains had got out of the way except the rear end ot a coal train which was just shunt ing. Into this the paisenger train train dashed with a crash that was heard for miles around, knocking the coal cars in all directions. The passengers were badly shaken, and some were bruised, but none were killed. But where was the brave driver ? From under the wreck of the overturned engine he was taken an hour afterwards, crushed and dying, but still able to speak. "Is the Pres;dent safe ?" he gasped. " Yes, and every. body else," was the answer. " Thank God for that," he said, and never spoke again. A splendid deed, truly, yet there is not a driver in a hundred who would not have stood to his duty with the same fidelity. Exposed to all sorts of weather, to con stant danger, and laden with responsibility, the engine drivers have a commendable record, and deserve higher appreciation both by the companies and by the public. "I am an engine driver," says Edward Roberts, " and have been for eleven years. My health was always good until July, 1885. Then something came over me that I couldn't account for. I felt tired, sleepy, and languid. My stomach felt sour and cold, my mouth tasted awfully bad, and my tongue was thickly coated. A disagreeable fluid came up into my mouth, and my appetite failed. No food, however light, agreed with me, and I had great pain after eating anything at all. In ten minutes my stomach would be all in a ferment, and swell like as a balloon does when the gas is running into it. I had also a miserable tightness around my chest and sides. Later on I had awful pain in the kidneys. I could not rest at night; I had dreadful drea ms, and would turn and turn in bed, but found no ease.

As he was passing the door, the defendant threw a quantity of paraffin oil which went upon his clothes causing a very offensive smell. Complainant, in cross-exam ination, said he did not see her throw the , but had been told afterwards that she paraffin, but it. At the Gerbals Police Court, on Saturday womb& a conviction under the bye-laws lately published by the Ma gistrate. of Glasgow, for regulating hackney coaches and Oiler carriages, took place before the witting magistrate. kona the evidence, it appeared that a gentleman residing in Milton Place, Laurieston,engaged a minibus on the street on friday night to carry him, in the first instance, to his own residence; and with the view of being immediately after wards taken to a dinner party in Abbotsford Mace, he wished to detain the vehicle, and intimated the same to the driver. The driver stated that he would not be detained by any man beyond his own allotted time, and as he had a fare to pick up in another quarter he refused to wait; on which the gentleman told him that he could not allow him , to go Until he had taken him to his destination, and that , being now engaged he was entitled to keep him the time prescribed by the bye-laws of the magistrates. The driver retorted angrily—demanded his fare for the distance he had come—kicked up a rumpus in the lobby of the house, and latterly refused to go away. The result was that the Pollee were called in and took him to the office, and on Sa turday morning he was fined in one guinea for refusing to comply with the clause of the bye-law issued by the Magis trates, which provides that a vehicle may be detained a cer tain given time (on payment) at the option of the hirer.

text: CENTRAL BUILDING FUND. Mr. Gray said, it was proposed that there should be a special collection for the Building Fund. He moved that it be referred to a committee. A committee was accordingly appointed to prepare an act relative to the collections. SABBATH OBSERVANCE. Mr. Balfour, W.S., brought up the report of Om Sabbath Observance Committee. He stated that the subject was growing in public interest, and it could not be more fully exhibited than in the fate of Mr. Locke's bill. While the cause, however, had been making progress, the committee were quite aware that it had met with reverses; but being prepared for those things, it only served to stimulate them to greater exertions. One of the reverses to which he would refer, was the opening of the Scottish Central Railway to the public on the Sabbath, and the committee could not re port that any of the Sabbath-breaking lines had been closed. He did not despair of success in these companies, and his great reason for this was, that he never could limit the providence of God. It must be seen that He had interfered most signally on the English lines. The Mayor of York had refused to take the chair vacant by the retirement of Mr. Hudson, and, rather than lose his services, it had been resolved to shut the line on the Sabbath. That circum stance alone ought to give the Church more confidence. Another ground for hope was in the fact that the Sabbath traffic did not meet the expenditure, and he was satisfied that the directors would not continue to run trains at a loss. Mr. Nixon proposed the adoption of the report, and the re-appointment of the committee. Mr. Lyon seconded the motion. He referred to Mr. Locke's statement, that on Easter Sunday 31 private two-horse car riages, 13 private one-horse carriages, and 149 public cabs, had attended four kirks or meeting-houses in the Lothian Road. He held in his hand a certificate by the inspector of hackney coaches for the city stating, that the whae num ber of licensed hackney coaches and cabs in the city amounted to 190; that on Easter Sunday 65 of these were employed by parties to attend the four churches in the Lothian Road ; that 178 parties were set clown that day at these churches; that the greatest number of cabs present at the Lothian Road at any one time did not exceed 30; that by far the greatest number of vehicles were employedby the congregation attending St. John's Episcopal Chapel, and very few by the other churches, and that it was the practice of families attending the principal Scottish Episcopal chapels to employ carriages on Easter Sunday who never used a carriage on any other Sunday throughout the year. On Easter Sunday one of the principal cab proprietors had 4.5 app ications for cabs, while the average number of ap plications on Sunday was only about ten. Mr. Blackadder said, there was no denying that cabs and carriages were used to an unnecessary extent on the Sabbath. He urged the members of the Free Church to abstain from the practice of using hired and private car riages on that day. Their people should not forget that this was just as much a desecration of the Sabbath as using any other means of travelling. After some further discussion, the motion of Mr. Nixon was approved of. The Assembly then took up the report of the manse building fund. The income for the past year was £111,748 7s. 61, a sum very far short of the proportionate instalment that the year should produce, and would have been inade quate had it not been for the large balance remaining over from last year, and that a number of congregations had not been in circumstances to apply for the grants allotted them. text: DECLINE OF COUNTRY TOWNS. Country towns are daily losing theiasysiognosay. The sur- " face becomes Smoother, like that of our current oohs, till, by the evenness of the superfioes, the value is lessened. Mail coaches did much, and railroads are doing more, to destroy all local charac teristics and distinctions. The two capitals of thesister kingdoms are divided by only four-and-twenty hours eassh, from the metro polis; and the interstitial towns, now that they receive the gos sip of London wet from the press, and new fashions and new follies bright from the mint, have flung aside those quaint old garments of individuality, which rendered Winchester as different from York, as Chester from all other cities of the Coiled Kingdom. It may be doubted whether they alter for the better. A man may cease to be they eoman without becoming the 'gentleman. Superficial polish is often acquired, when the nature is not intrinsically improved. The heartiness of the country disappears, but the poldness ef the I capital lags behind. The common run of towns resembles • blunt razor, or a single-barrelled gun, or a sailing-packet, or any other , antediluvian thing which,instead of beguiling the time, by looking I like the time, looks like times better forgotten. Its society is a shoal of minnows, among which the most moderate fish becomes • Triton. Accustomed to receive its laws and opinions, like its ribbons and other manufactured goods, from London, if you ask a emotion, people are as slow in answering as if waiting the snivel of the coach to make up their minds. A century ago, ere roads and newspapers had established an electric chain betwixt thecapi tal and her satellites, every country town was the capital of her province, as In France at the present day; and the substantial old mansion-houses now figuring as boarding ; schools and manufac tories, atteat that, nforetime, the winter migration of their squire archy extended no further than the limits of their shire. The wealth thus concentrated brought refinement and progress. Now, I all who have money to spend, spend it in London; and country towns are, consequently, restricted to a secondary order of civilisa tion. The great manufacturing towns are distinguished by a cer tain flashiness of taste, in addition to their smoke, noise, and unwholesome-looking population. The cathedral towns pretend to higher gentility, are blue and scandalous, addicted to whist and green tea. Garrison towns are gay and flirtatious, inclining to theatricals, and boating a capital circulating library. But the genuine country town is the one that hath neither canon nor can non, neither black coats nor red, neither a barrack nor cathedral clone; nor even a manufactory, beyond a slender steam-engine chimney or two, starting up, like asparagus running to seed, in the suburbs; or, perhaps, a few miles, half hidden, among the shallows of an unnavigable river.—Mrs. Gore is the New Monthly

text: Dr. Temple recently held a visitation at Torrington (North Devon); and while his carriage was being har nessed for the return journey to Barnstaple intimated that he woad "walk on." The Bishop took the old, hilly road, which is now but little used, and the coach man unaware of this fact drove off, yin Bideford, quite in another direction. For five miles his lordship trudged on, and becoming fatigued, and seeing no sign of his carriage, on arriving at Newton Tracey he asked a respectable publican and farmer there to give him a lift." Boniface had a cart, but the cart was unlicensed, and he pleaded this objec tion against complying with Dr. Temple's wish. But the Bishop was equal to the emergency; he was desirous to proceed, and would pay the cost of a licence. This anxiety aroused the publican's suspicions, who rejoined that if his visitor would "sit down and take a drop o' summat " he would go to Barnm and get a licence. But for this preliminary the Bishop could not wait, and urged his host to harness his cart at once and take out a licence on reaching Barnstaple. More convinced than ever of the character and occupation of the pedestrian, Boniface broke out, emphasising his denunciation with sundry strange oaths, "I know thee! Thou'rt one of they supervisor fellows that are always going about the country trying to trap poor folk about their carts." The astonished prelate mildly endeavoured to assuage the wrath of the irate publican by the statement that he was the Bishop of Exeter. `No thin' o' the sort!" retorted the other, "you won't trick nie as you did my neighb ur Vother week, and get me fined £5." So the Bishop had again to sally forth, until he was picked up, about four miles from his destination, by the carriage which•had, in the meanwhile, been sent out in quest of him from Barn stable. "lie wor got up like a sort o' gentleman varmer, wi' a pair o' gaiters or breeches, and a rummy sort o' hat, but he wor one o' they Excise chaps, and I warn% goite to be done, 'cause you see my neighbour was fined Vother day for taking his wife out for a drive." ENGLAND AND THE SULTAN OF Mounocco.---By the new treaty the Queen may appoint one or more Consuls in the dominions of the Emperor, and both they and the Charge d'Aftaires shall be inviolable both in person and house. Each shall have the liberty of establishing a place of worship, to be protected by the British fig. The next article gives the important right of freely travelling through the Sultan's territory. Any British subject shall have the right to pass through or reside in any part of his Majesty's dominions, subject only to the same regulations as are submitted to by the citizens of the most favourecA nations. Furthermore, British subjects shall have the right of freely hiring houses, and may claim to be assisted in so doing by the Moorish authorities. They shall not be obliged to pay under any pretence what ever, any taxes or impositions. They shall be exempt from all military service, whether by land or sea, from forced loans, and from every extraordinary contribution. Their dwellings shall be respected; no arbitrary searches shall be made, no examination of books and papers, except with the orders and consent of the Consul-General or Consul. " And, generally, his Majesty the Sultan engages that the subjects of b - .r Britannic Majesty residing in his estates or doce]nions, shall enjoy their property and personal see:arity in as full and ample a manner as subjects of the Emperor of Morocco are entitled to do within the territories of her Britannic Majesty." Two articles relate to the manner of carrying on trade, and then comes a stipulation which seems likely to be made whenever civilised men come in contact with Mussulman law. All criminal causes, and all civil differences occurring between British subjects, shall be decided by the British Consul General or his deputy, and no governor, oadi, or other Moorish authority shall intermeddle therein. In cases between a British and a Moorish subject the matter shall be referred to, the authorities of the country to which the defendant belongs. If the defendant be a Moor, the matter goes before the Cadi, the British Consul being present; if the defendant be an Englishman, the case is tried by the Consul, the Governor or Cadi being present. The Consul General and the Moorish Minister of Foreign Affairs are This singular regulation is j de rived?dgs from the d l a e s , r c e a s p o ft t u . lations " between the European Powers and Turkey, and whatever may be the case at Con stantinople, it is suited to the circumstances of such an empire as Morocco. text: EXCURSION TRIPS.—This year the number of persons who have left the town during the feast holidays shows a great increase upon previous years. Mr. Phillips, station master of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Market-place Station, informs us that last Saturday the number of ordinary passengers who booked was 1,420, and of excur sionists 227. On Monday, 649 ordinary passengers left, and an excursion to Blackpool, given by Messrs. Day, Nephew, and Son, took out 506 trippers. The following day—Tuesday—the number of ordinary passengers was 1,890, excursionists 616 ; Primitive Methodist first train to Blackpool and Isle of Man 1,024, second do. 821, third do. (an overflow train sent off by the company) 632. About 1,000 persons were left behind, there being no coaches to take them. Springfield excursions to Black pool, 1,000; St. Peter's, Earlsheaton, and St. John's, Dewsbury Moor, to Bridlington, 800. The ordinary traffic on Wednesday and Thursday was very heavy, and great credit is due to the officials for the promptitude wills which the various trains were got off. We are not aware that any casualties have occurred. Only two excursion trips went from the London and North-Western Station, one being to Blackpool, which conveyed 365 passengers; and the other to Bangor, taking 65. The ordinary traffic on the 25th numbered 1,801 passengers, and on the following day 1,006. Under the superintendence of Mr. Reeves, the station master, aided by the energetic porters, &c., the trains were despatched and arrived without accident to anyone. The returns from the Great Northern Station show that on Saturday last there were booked 1,630 ordinary and 96 excursionists ; on the Monday 139 excursionists and 968 ordinary. Trips were run on the Tuesday to Skegness, Boston, Ramsgate, Saltburn, Ripen, Sheffield, Scarbro', and Bodnar, and 3,248 persons availed themselves of the opportunity to visit the places. The ordinary traffic the same day was 1,405. THE VOLUNTEERS AT SEEGNESS.—On Saturday after noon last the Fifth West Yorkshire Rifle Volunteers, which include detachments from Wakefield, Goole, Dews bury, and Batley, left their respective towns for a week's encampment at Skegness, which is now fast becoming the most popular sea-side resort on the Lincolnshire coast. The Dewsbury detachment paraded at headquarters shortly after noon, and marched along Northgate to the Great Northern Station. They were joined by the Wake field detachments, arriving in Skegness about five o'clock. An advanced party, consisting of about 40 men selected from the various detachments, proceeded to Skegness on the 20th inst. to take over the camp equipage and make general arrangements. During the encampment the town has been visited by a large number of excursionists from Dewsbury, Batley, and other places. The camp has been laid out in a most complete manner, and it is considered to be, the best the corps has bad during their 12 annual encampments. The battalion is under the command of Lieut.-Col. Sheard, and among the other officers present at the camp are Major Lee, Major and Adjutant Townley, acting Major Capt. Wright, Capts. Fox, Nor wood, Mayman, Thompson, and Mackenzie; Lieuts. Beverley, Fox, Blakeley, Carter, and Taylor, and Dr. F. Wood. This is the first time the corps has visited Skeg ness, and it is gratifying to know that the men are highly delighted with the place. On Sunday morning divine service was conducted on the race ground by the Rev. L. S. Calvert, M.A.., Headmaster of Batley Grammar School. On Monday morning the men commenced their week's work, and fortunately they have been favoured with very fine weather. Entertainments have been given at the camp theatre several evenings during the week, and the men have appeared to enjoy their visit. The corps were inspected yesterday morning by Col. Hardy, of the Pontefract Military centre, and this afternoon the camp will break up. Messrs. Bennett and Co., of Doncaster, are the refreshment contractors, and they have given the greatest satisfaction. The conduct of the men reflects great credit on the towns from which they come, and West Yorkshire has cause to be proud of her citizen soldiers. The number under canvas is about 550.

Between these two the people who do not go to extremes, but know that there are times when doors and windows should be shut, and times when they should be open, have a very hard time of it. The fresh air crank—usually a lady—gets up on a winter morning, spreads her bedding upon the window-sill, thiows all the windows up, sets the door back, and is heard ejaculating, "What a lovely, fresh morning V' by the 'people who have dashed out of their warm rooms into the cool draught she has created on the stairs and in the entries, and who enter the dining-room shivering. Ten to one she has pulled the window half down there. Tropical fashions go with her into the frozen regions. She enjoys riding in a coach with both windows open, sitting in the crack of an outer door after dancing, welcoming wild winas that blow away the hearth rugs and cause the pictures on the walls to rook to and fro. She is responsible for all the bad colds in the family, and for heaven knows what lung complaints and influenzas amongst those who have the misfortune to be her fellow passengers on public conveyances. For if there is a window, up it goes; if there is a door, it must fly open, regardless of blast or tempest. Nevertheless, she is always boasting of her love of ',fresh air, and uttering her belief that if people would only do as she does they would be as well, as happy and as wise.
