text: For the first time the Metropolitan Railway Company on Friday presented for inspection its system of electric traction. A week's trial has established the train as a train in being, aud on Friday it worked as smoothly, as completely, as though the electrical system on the Underground Railway had been a fact for months. The train, apart from the fact that it is enabled to dispense with the conventional engine, differs little from any ordinary train. It begins with a glass box in which a man turns the wheel that controls the motive power. Forming part of the coach in which is the motor is a compartment for passengers. built on the American plan, with low-backed seats and a central passage. That, however, is a com partmeut by itself. The rest of the train consists of the ordinary everyday carriages, first, second, and third class, according to custom. In all, its capacity is for 312 passengers. text: Funeral reform is a subject that is demanding fresh attention every day. The absurd burlesque of grief, as represented by our modern para phernalia, brought into requisition upon the burial of a person is enough, were not its sur roundings of so solemn a character, to excite ridicule; as it is, it can only create a feeling of sadness. A procession of some six or eight utter strangers to the man who has passed away, arrayed in dingy cloaks, bearing superannuated policemen's staffs. A ricketty hearse driven by a still more ricketty coachman. Two or three old coaches, groaning as if mourning for the dead. Horses that evidently ought to have gone to their own last home—at the kennels. And " foUowers" in cotton-silk hat-bands look ing upon it dolsomely as a most inconvenient and tiresome call upon them. These are the con comitants of an every-day funeral in England, which, if we are to believe the utterances of the clergyman over the poor remains, should par take of an exactly opposite character. We are glad to find the Salisbury Diocesan Synod has taken the matter up, and a Committee have made a number of recommendations, of which the following is an abstract : "With regard to mourning apparel, they recom mend that long flowing hatbands, scarves, and cloaks be altogether disused, but that plain hatbands of crape or cloth be retained; and these, as well as mourning apparel in general, they consider the mourner should provide for himself. This is recommended (1) as a more decided proof of sympathy, (2) to save expense at a time when the demands upon the family are often neccessarily heavy. And here they would discourage the old custom of giving away complimentary mourning at the time of the funeral. They strongly urge the clergy to decline all such gifts. A clause to this effect appears in a circular letter on the general subject of Funeral Reform from clergy to their parishioners in the deanery of Marlborough. Thus any odium that an individual clergyman might incur from refusing such gifts while Ins brethren accepted them would be avoided. And in general they recommend that the apparel of mourners be simple, plain, and expensive. But in making these suggestions, the Committee would guard themselves against the imputation of deprecating the proper use of mourning apparel, which they desire may ever be worn as a token of sympathy and loving sorrow." Surely, with this no one can quarrel.

text: Henry Pelham, it is true, was by no means a con temptible person. His understanding was that of Walpole on a somewhat smaller scale. Though not a brilliant orator, he wan, like his master, a good de bater, a good parliamentary tactician, a good man of business. Like his snorter, he distinguished himself by the neatness and clearness of his financial expositions. Here the resemblance ceased. Their characters were altogether dissimilar. Walpole was good-humoured, but would have his way his spirits were high, and his manners frank even to coarseness. The temper of Pelham was yielding, but peevish : his habits were regular, and his deportment strictly decorous. Wal pole was constitutionally fearless, Pelham constitution ally timid. Walpole had to face a strong opposition; but no mass in the Government durst wag a finger against him. Almost all the opposition which Pelham bad to encounter was from members of the Government stf which he was the head. His own paymaster spoke against his estimates. His own secretaty-at-wor spoke against his Regency Bill. In one day Walpole turned Lord Chesterfield, Lord Burlington, and Lord Clinton out of the royal household, dismissed the highest tones of Scotland from their posts, and took away the regiments of the Duke of Bolton and Lord Cobham, be cause he suspected them of having encouraged the resistance to the Excise Bill. He would far rather Pave contended with the strongest minority, under the ablest leaders, than have tolerated mutiny in his own party. It would have gone hard with any of his col leagues mho had ventured, on a Government question, to divide the House of Commons against him. Pelham. on the other hand, was disposed to bear anything rather than drive from office any man round whom a new opposition could form. text: IN DEATH !car DIVIDED.—The death is recorded at Aberystwith, at the age of 92, of Matthew Marsh. lje entered the navy when a youth, and afterwards the army, and served in the battle of Waterloo, where he lost the tip of one of his fingers, which was struck by a bell. He marched to Paris, and was afterwards for some time in India. Returning to England, he lived in Kent, and afterwards removed to South Wales, where he was engaged for very many years in driving coaches, which occupation he gave up when the railway was opened to Aberyst with, twenty-two years ago. His wife, who had been completely paralysed for a couple of years, and upon whom he attended with the utmost devotion, died only on Sunday week, and was buried on the following Thursday. During the last year or two he had gradually weakened, and on the 2nd inst., when told of his wife's death, he became unconscious, and remained in that state until the end.

text: INAUGURATION OF THE MAIL COACHES SERVICE. The parcels mail service by road between Liverpool a nd MancheStat was inaugurated on Monday night, ' when the first coach to be despatched from either places I started on its journey. The departure of the, coach from the Liverpool office was witnessed by a lai crowd, who cheered it heartily, as it left the post office yard. The tune allowed for the journey between Liverpool and Manchester is a little over five hours, the coach leaving at ten at night, aad being timed to arrive at its destin ation at 3.15. a.m.,.allowing for an average rate of tra velling of seven miles an hour. The coach on Monday night was drawn by three magnificent bays, and the turn out presented a very smart appearance, the driver (Henry Buckley) and the guard (John Thomas) being seated on the box. The first stopping place out of Liverpool is Preacot, where horses are changed. At War rington the mail is met by a parcel post van from Wigan, and after Warrington is left horses.are again changed 1 at Hollins-green. The guards of both coaches, who are old soldiers, are suppded with horns to herald the ap- I proacb of their coaches, after the fashion of old coaching days. They are also armed with a sword bayonet and six-chambered revolver, to defend the mails in case of an attask by highway men. A large number of the prin cipal as well as subordinate officials of Canning-place assembled to witness the despatch of the first mail, a vigorous blast being blown on the horn by Thomas as the coach was driven away. The coach from Manchester to Liverpool started punc tually at ten o'clock from the parcel office in Stevenson square, some thousands of people having assembled there to witness the inauguration of the service. The van was well filled with parcels, and its departure, which was announced by the blowing of a horn, was loudly cheered by the crowd of people. The vehicle was , followed down the main streets of the city by some hundreds of spectators. In connection with the new ; service a single horse mail coach is run between South port and Liverpool and vice versa, calling at Formby, Blundellsands, Waterloo, Seaforth, and Bootle.

text: IT was impossible to behold, as we happened to do, the eager crowds that filled the streets in the neighbourhood of the railway station, and to know, as we did, that they had assembled to cheer and to welcome the pugilistic " champion," without being impressed by such a scene as a living indication of the love of Englishmen for English bravery. For this, we verily believe, was the real feeling that was predominant with the very populace on that occasion. They exhi bited a sort of hero-worship—such as it was; and "the god of their idolatry" was a prize-fighter. But he was, in their eyes, on that very account, a brave man ; and as such they admired, nay, adored him with enthusiasm. The arrival of this their hero was patiently waited for by the people for several hours ; and when, at length, the train that had the honour of conveying no less distin guished a personage than Tom SAYERS, " the Champion of England," arrived at the station, and he had been transferred to the coach that was in readiness to take him to his hotel, such was their reverence for him, that they could not refrain from taking away the horses, and, as many of them as could contrive to yoke themselves to the vehicle, proceeding to draw him in triumph through the streets. Now these devoted people, be it remembered, were altogether of the work ing classes. They must have sacrificed, mast if not all of them, at least a half-day's work—which, of course, means a half-day's wages each—to the interesting opportunity of paying homage to one whom they doubtless considered worthy of it in kis character as a pugilist. And they were Englighmen all over, in thus doing honour to whom, in their estimation, honour was so pre eminently due. The word hero is defined to be "a man eminent for bravery." And here, they felt, was a hero of the true English stamp. " Eminent for bravery," popularly considered, such an one must undoubtedly be. text: It is many years since any public event has made itself so, evident in the streets of London as the funeral of the late Duke of Clarence. Everywhere the number of people dressed in black was noticeable, blinds were drawn down at all the public buildings and in many private houses, there were shutters before the windows of the great majority of shops, and flags on almost every flagpost at half-mast, even to the little "Jacks "which decorate certain omnibuses. The Stock Exchange did not open, and some shops were closed thdotwhole day ; but it was not until noon that the demonstration became most remarkable. The scene in the city after midday was more striking. Shops and warehouses were closed, and by a common impulse all the streams of traffic which struggled unceasingly in Cheapside, Fleet-street, and other City thoroughfares seemed turned in one direction. The employ - es steamed in hundreds from the great places of business in their working clothes and mingled with the crowds of mourners who came in cabs, omnibuses, and on foot from all points of the compass and thronged th e streets leading to St. Paul's. By one o'clock the grea t area of St. Paul's Churchyard was filled by a mor or less motley crowd, which increased every momente At three o'clock the Lord Mayor and Sheriffs arrived in State coaches, the brilliant colours of the vehicles and the liveries showing even more resplendent than usual against the sombre backgrdusd. A way was made. The great west door was thrown open, and in decorous silence the civic dignitaries entered. Many of the crowd then left; but many thousands remained outside during the whole service, those favourably placed catching occasional glimpses of the interior as the door opened and fainting or hysterical women were carried out. With the conclusion of the service the crowd slowly dis persed. At four o'clock some of the business establish ments reopened, but the gloom of the day still pervaded the wholecity. Almost every theatre and place of entertafiiinent was dosed' at night, and neither nieetings nor social festivities were held. Throughout the country, and in the chief cities of the Continent„ as well as of India and the British Colonies solemn memorial services were held.

On the 22nd of August last, the first day of the annual regatta, on the irwell, the plaintiff was proceeding in the defendant's omnibus from Deansgate to the Pomona Gardens, The usual terminus of the omnibus was the Egertoyrarms, belt on the occasion of the regatta, it was the invariAle practice to continue the journey as far as the Pomona Gardens. On arriving at the Egerton Hotel, an altercation took place between the plaintiff and the conductor, Dixon, the plaintiff not being pro vided with the amount of his fare; and ,the result was that Dixon seized the plaintiff by the collar, dragged him out of the omnibus, and threw him upon the road. At the moment he was . thrown out of the omnibus, a han som-cab, also the property of the defendant Greenwood, was being driven along the road, and it passed over the plaintiff: His legs and ankles were severely fractured. and his Bead was much crushed, the skull being laid bare some six inches. text: MRS. LANGTRY is at home in New York once more. She has travelled far into the West, purchased ranches, become a citizen, played Galatea to the red men, captured cowboy heart, and done everything but vote. In the softly-shaded candlelight, wrapped in Oriental silks, and very fair to see, she told the other evening of her experiences during her second trip to the Pacific shores. Her house in West Twenty-third -street was ready to receive her when she returned somewhat later than is considered proper in well-regulated households. "I am an American now, for I have made my declaration," continued the Lily, gleefully, as though she enjoyed it hugely. "Then I set off fire crackers on the Fourth of July, gave lots of them to the boys, and had a big flag on my house in 'Frisco. Little uonse, great big flag, so big that I could not see out of the windows, but that didn't matter, did it I was ill, though, and could not recite, as I promised. That was so unlucky, wasn't it? But I have made all my people take out their papers and become Americans, That's right, isn't it ?" Mrs. Langtry is a very bright conversationalist, and has a charming way of putting questions at the end of her sentences. She told how she had enjoyed all the sights, visited fruit farms, and ridden on stage-coaches through dangerous passes where horrid highwaymen hid waiting for beautiful stars to carry off to their strongholds. "But I did not see the highwaymen," she added in a somewhat reproachful tone. It might have been a novel way of having one's diamonds stolen, but the Lily scorned the suggestion, and declared that both she and the driver of the coach had been badly scar d." "Oh by the way, I've bought a ranche, don't you know 2" she said in the same tone that one would announce the pur chase of a poodle. " It's big-7,ooojacres ; almost as large as the island on which I was born. It is situated in Lake and Nappa counties." Then Mrs. Langtry talked about things theatrical. "1 have not entirely made up my mind about my plays next season. text: Many and curious are the customs regarding brides. In Switzerland (says a contemporary) the bride on her wedding-day will permit no one, not even her parents, to kiss her upon the lips. In parts of rural England the cook pours hot water over the thres hold after the bridal couple have gone in order to keep it warm for another bride. The pretty custom of throwing the slipper originated in France. An old woman, seeing the carriage of her young King—Louis Xlll.—passing on the way from church, where he had just been married, took off her shoe, and flinging it at his coach, cried out: " 'Tis all I have, your Majesty, but may the blessing of God go with it." There is an old superstition in Germany against marriages in May. A favourite wedding day ., in Scotland is December 31st, so that the young couple can leave their old life with the old year, and begin their married with the new one. The Italians permit no wedding gifts that are sharp and pointed, con nected with whioh practice is our super stition that the gift of a knife severs friendship. One marriage custom is that of the bride, immediately after the ceremony, flinging her bouquet among her maiden friends. She who catches it is destined to be the next bride.

Barnes, the Deputy Coroner for West minster, has held an inquiry into the circumstances I attending the death of Henry John Ebers, aged 60 years, a coach painter, who was found dead in bed at 61, Berwick-street, Oxford-street, on the morning of July 26. Born of a Lancashire family in the year 1811, in a village where the name of Primitive Methodism had left a strong impression, Mr. Collier was trained in that faith, and early showed an aptitude for preaching. Robert Barclay & Co. of the Stobcross slip Docks, have applied for, and obtained the use of the dredging machines, &c., in order to the putting up a new slip of 800 tons at their works. The advantage of such a slip must be evident, allowing, as it will do the masters, owners, and underwriters to inspect vessels' bottoms in our own port, previous to loading, instead of going to Greenock or Port-Glasgow for the purpose. text: On Monday evening the East George Matthews delivered his popular lecture entitled " Grit, " at the Bible Christian Chapel, Oxford street, Swansea. Coomillor W. Pike presided, and, after a few introductory words, called upon the Roy. George Matthews. The rev, gentle man said he Intended to enlarge upon a quality which was needed at the Government, and in the paths of science and literature, needed in the daily Press, and needed in the Church of God. All men needed that quality—high, undaunted resolu tion ; or, to put it in short, sharp Saxon, grit. If a man elected to mount the range of the world's ladder he must, as Charles Lamb had said, have grit; and the man who wished to cultivate that quality must become a pugilist.. that is, he must knock the eyes out of all "ifs." Beethoven's favourite motto was:.." Barriers are not made to say to an aspiring genius, Thus far, and no further. " When the Emperor Napoleon was informed that the Alps stood in the 'way of his army he said, "Then there shall be no Alps," hence the construction of the road across - the Simplon. The lecturer then dilated on difficul ties, portraying in vivid colones the life-work of William Carey, the Apostle of India, as an in stance of what a man with true grit could sur mount, and proceeded to say that there were no cherries without stones, no roses without thorns; and the person who avoided the hive because the bees have stings, did not deservethe honey-comb. John Ruskin had said that one of his calamities was that in early life he had nothing to endure; and Beethoven had said of a man that he pos sessed the stuff to make a genius in the musical world,. if only, when a boy, he had been well flogged. It was the defeat that trained the general, and not the victory . . Washington lost more battles than he gamed victories, but it was well known how he had suc ceeded in the end. Misfortune was a rough nurse, but she reared giants. An old proverb said that crosses were the ladders that led to heaven. True grit was never lazy or idle. It had no sympathy in the world with the senti ments of the boy in America, who used to sing : "I wish I was the President Of the United States; I never would do nothing ' But swing on all the gates." (Laughter.) Men must work hard if they would rise. As Longfellow had well said, men did not go to Paradise in coaches. The shells which the sea threw up on the shore were not the best; the pearls had to be divided after. The real man was God—made, self made, not man—made. The lecturer anath ematised those young men who expected the world to give them a living without working, and asked if some one Would invent and inflict a painless lock-jaw until that class of young fellows found out that it was their duty to work for their own bread? (Hear, hear.) True grit was sticking to it. The men who had moved the world had been persevering, self- , reliant, and indefatigable. Honest purpose was next touched upon. The young man who handled the yard stick should not allow his conscience to be longer than the measuring article, nor broader than the ribbon. The saying that a man could not suc ceed in business, and be honest, was as old as the devil, and about as much to be believed. If , a person could not maintain his integrity and succeed, it were better he maintain his integrity and low. (Cheers.) The lecturer then enu merated various men who had risen to the pinnacles of fame through resolution, and asked the young men present to emulate their characters.

text: On Saturday night the Belfast boat train which runs between Manchester and Fleetwood, on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, met with a most disastrous accident, the whole train, oonsisting of an engine and nine coaches, being utterly wrecked. Happily comparatively few passengers received injury, though in the circum stances it is miraculous that there is not a fearful tale of death to record. The train, on leaving Chorley, ran into and through a large mass of earth, which through the action of the recent excessive rains, had fallen from the embankment on to the line, and was completely wrecked. About a mile north of the station the Lancashire and Yorkshire line runs through a deep cutting, part of which is tunnelled. On the other side of this tunnel the cutting or gorge is con tinued for about 300 yards, the steep declivity on either side being supported by massive stone retaining walls, nearly 30ft. high, strengthened by gt series of flying arches. Between the tunnel and the high walls there runs a lower retaining wall flush with the escapement, and at this point there was a large landslip some time on Saturday night. The sandy soil had become saturated with water, and a large mass had fallen on the down line. It was stated that the declivity had been frequently inspected, and reported on during the week, though it was not considered to present signs of immediate danger. The boat train left Chorley at a few minutes to eight o'clock for Preston, and dashed at the rate of 30 miles an hour through the clayey obstruction, emerging from which the train was unable to regain the rails, and went with impetuous leaps and bounds, ploughing its way over the ballast and sleepers for a distance of 60 yards, only being stopped from toppling completely over by the wall, which it grazed all the way. The driver—Henry Southworth--promptly shut off steam, and almost simultaneously the train divided, the automatic brake being brought into action, and the train came to a standstill. 'lite train was composed of nine carriages and the engine, and the side of every carriage against the wall was smashed in, some of the timbers being split like matchwood. Cox, the guard of the train, had a wonderful escape, for a huge stone weighing about 3cwt., displaced from the retaining wall, crashed through the middle of the van, almost at his side. The rails were torn up for a considerable distance. The train was well filled with passengers, who were thrown into a state of fearful excitement, and were knocked about the compartments with great violence caused by the jolting of the train over the sleepers. Fortunately, comparatively few received serious injury, which, to say tile least, is very remarkable. Although the carriages were knocked about so disastrously, the gas remained lighted, and this tended somewhat to allay the passengers' terrible state of tension. It was found that only eight persons sustained bruises. The worst cases were those of Mr. Peter Cosgrove, of the Roslee Poet Office, Fermanagh, Ireland, whom it was found necessary to take to the Bolton Infirmary; Mr. Edward Bennion, who resides at 19, Brown-street, Withington, Manchester, who was also seriously hurt; and Henry Southworth, the engine driver, and Henry Riding, the stoker, who sustained severe shocks, but were able to proceed home in a short time. The up line la i z e luickly cleared, and the passengers of the w train were trans ferred to a ' Preston train, which was placed alongside, and proceeded on to Fleetwood several of the sufferers having been attended to by a doctor who was in the train. It was not till after 11 o'clock that a breakdown train with a gang of men arrived, and at once proceeded to clear the debris. They worked throughout the night in heavy rain, but the lines were not cleared for traffic until half-past one on Sunday afternoon.

text: Panshanger, left by the last Earl Ccrwper to his widow, who died on Sunday last, though not an ancient house, posse%es many interesting amocia tions, and stands in the midst, of a beautiful park, famous for its oak trees. The mansion, about mid way between Cole 'Green and Ifertingfordbury Stations, is built on rising ground, with charming views in every direction. It was at Colne, or, as it is new written, Cole Green, close by, that the first Lord Cowper, in the reign of Queen Anne, seeking a country home not too distant from town, built himself a moderate-sized residence, and lived there until the date of death in 1723. This was occupied successfully by the third and fourth earls, but the fifth successor to the title. in 1801 took the original edifice down and built, as the family seat, a house on higher ground, about a mile to the northward. Modern Panshanger house is not architecturally perfect, reflecting too many of the faults common to the period of its construction, but it is a hand some pile, and adds a picturesque feature to the surrounding park. ! This charming stretch of woodlands, as stated, is remarkable for its timber, the most famous tree being the historic Parishanger Oak, a landmark as long ago as the commencement of the eighteenth century, and still vigorous. Within; the picture gallery contains a fine series of works of the Florentine school, mostly collected by the third earl, who settled in' Florence in. 1762, was there created a Prince of the Holy Doman Empire, and spent most of his life in the city. In the middle of the last century Panshanger, owing, amongst other causes, to its convenient distance from town, became a centre of political life, and welcomed many of the most distinguished states men of the day. Palmerston delighted in it; Talleyrank and - Esterhaz - y were often guests of Earl Cowper, with 'Lords John Russell, Melbourne, and others. Some twenty-four miles from Westminster, the coaches took half a. day to do the journey, accom plishing in six hours what an ordinary train now does in under an hour. But this proved no hind- ! ranee to those who made Panshinger a social and Political meeting-place. text: RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT GUILDFORD. A serious railway collision occurred at Guildfonl Shortly before midnight on Thursday. A heavily laden goods train on the way to Portsmouth was nearing Guildford station when the 10.50 passenger train from Redhill for Reading ran into it. The latter, having just left the station, Nsas not travel ling at full speed, but the impact was sufficient to throw the passengers across the compartments. Several waggons of the goods train were overturned. and the sides of some of the passenger coaches were tom open. The trains were brought to a standstill, and the terrified passengers, seine Sf whom sprang from the train, were conducted back to the station, all of them having fortunately escaped serious harm; but the guard of the goods train was taken to the hospital. A few minutes later several coaches of the last South-Western train from Waterloo to Guildfonl went of the line near the same spot, without, however, causing any serious personal . . snjury.

NEWTON • RACES: INTERTNTING COMMENTS.— Speaking of Newton races, last week, a sporting contemporary observes; "If shorn of the import ance which once characterised the Cup Day at New ton, we nevertheless welcome it as an old friend; and we, who can remember witnessing the Newton Cup for nearly five and twenty years, could associ ate a world of Turf history with its decision that would read like a fairy tale to those who only know Lancashire racing in recent years. Who is there that can remember the opening of the Newton branch line from the main line, near Earlestown Jpnction, to the course. Who cannot recount the breakdown of the. engine, and the clambering up clay embankments, until the broadcloth then ob. tamable for suits was a compound of black-cloth and yellow-coloured mud. Ten, eleven, and twelve o'clock struck, and still the unlucky voyageurs had not returned to Manchester. The writer once re members his sire and a relative turning up in the early hours of the morning, in a state of mud and bewilderment not easily described. The branch line is now unused. It was condemned as unsafe some few years back, and now the direct way is either to Newton Bridge or to Earlestown Junction. The remainder of the distance must be eithernegotiated on shank's pony or by trap. In the days when the branch line was first used the county families drove to the Newton course in four-horsed coaches. They were the natural stands that were then in general use; and the erection of the Newton Grand Stand—one of the most commodious and best in the Kingdom —was quite an event in the district, whilst the hot dinners in its saloon were one of the proverbial features in a visit to Newton, for, no matter the heat, your, true-bred Lancastrian can always feed. Quicker communication has changed the pidnie character of the earlier Newton meetings to a purely business gathering, and the present generation of racing men have no more idea of the jolly meeting the Willow S furnished our fathers than they have of the pre-historic period, which is a cut above the imagination of those who have not a soul above the hacknbyed 'Six to four on the field,' which is so constantly dinned into our ears now-a- ' days."

Mr. Steel watched the interests of Joseph Pennington, engine driver, and William Fairclough, the signal man ; while Mr. Browne represented the widow. The , Coroner stated that on Thursday at about one o'clock Barrow was engaged in shunting operations at Bank Quay Station. He was instructed to detach a brake van from some coaches. He got between the van and the last coach for the purpose of unscrewing the couplings, but finding he could not do it be came out and gave the driver the signal to "ease up." Barrow again went between the van and the coach to unscrew the couplings, and while dilfig this the coach struck him in the back, causing him to fall on the rail and three of the coaches passed over him, injuring his arm badly.—Dr. Ilodgkinson, senior house surgeon at the Infirmary, said Barrow was suffering from fatty disease of the heart. Death was due to shock caused by the laceration of the arm muscles and contusion of the chest. Joseph Pennington, the engine driver in question, detailed the facts connected with the shunting opera tions, and said Barrow gave him the signal to set back." As soon as witness started the train he missed Barrow and immediately stopped. He got down from his engine and remained by the deceased until the ambulance arrived. A verdict of "Accidental death " was returned, and the driver was exonerated from all blame.

text: THE INUNDATION.—DREADFUL ACCIDENT ' . TO THE HEREFORD MAIL. The heavy rains which fell throughout the earlier part of last and concluding portion of the previous week, . caused extensive and destructive floods in different parts of England. On Friday afternoon week, the inhabitants of both banks of the Thames, at London, were driven from their houses in consequence of the tide rising higher than • it had done for several years. It rushed like a cataract over the various wharves, and in many cases filled time 44 basements of the houses. The occupants had to get out of the upper windows and drop into waggons or boats 1 that were taken to their rescue. The gardens of the Archbishop of Canterbury, at Lambeth, were covered with water, which was in some places five of six feet deep. r Hungerford market, the Templegardens, Great Scotland yard, and the arches under the Adelphi, were submurged, and much property was destroyed. At Market Har- , o borough, Leicestershire, a great flood occurred on the ' a. same day. A post office messenger was drowned. The , Crowmills viaduct on the Midland railway was partially i destroyed ; and a portion of the line at Loughborough was washed away. Factories and dwellings were flooded 7 in the vicinity of Leicestershire, the water rising eight feet above the ordinary level. Many cows, horses, pigs, 0 and sheep were drowned.—Hereford city and county . t , -,were devastated by a succession of floods occasioned by the rising of the rivers Wye, Lugg, and Frome. Before - daybreak on Friday morning the London mail was en ; , gu - lphed in the wreck of a fallen bridge; and, in addition to the loss of three of the horses, and serious injuries to the coachman, guard, arid passengers, one human life • was sacrificed. This occurred at a place called Fiven ' Bridges, Dormingto, six miles from Hereford. The / ' .. - coachman and box-1, issenger were thrown upon the : F ! ,4leaders, and having got among, some trees or hedges . kmianaged to save themselves from drowning. A few of the mail bags were recovered by means of a pole, but their contents are almost useless from wet. Thirteen bags, however, remained on or in the coach, and were floated with it and the two wheelers down the . bed of die Frame. Ita 11 ereford the gas works were .1 flooded, and the town, completely surrounded with water, 1 had die additional misfortune of remaining in darkness, . Newton Abbott's, Devonshire, suffered severely from the ' • rising of the Lemon and the Teign. The banks burst, . and property to a considerable amount was swept away ' or damaged. On the premises of Mr. Vicary, tanner, , property valued at 1:500 was destroyed. Several streets - were rendered impassable, and the inhabitants had to betake themselves to their upper rooms.—The Trent IValley line of railway has been completely under water, and the Tame brid ge , which crosses the Valley line near Lichfield, was carried away. text: THI? scene from the cars while passing through the Grand Canyon of the Arkansas is thus de scribed by the New Orleans Times-Democrat : "At times you can see a train approaching on what seems to be the opposite side of the narrow river. Looking out, you discover it to be your own train doubling a sharp turn in the canyon, the locomotive running so close to the rear coach thatit would not be a difficult matter to carry on a conversation between the two. Suddenly the walls come closer together, the river is crowded into a space only thirty feet wide, and the two precipices reach the height of 3,000 ft., rising almost vertically from the water's edge. The track, no longer able to find a foothold on the rock, is driven to a bridge running length wise of the chasm, suspended on iron trusses, morticed into the everlasting granite on either side. Here is the climax of sublimity. A foam ing torrent only twelve feet beneath you, walla that may almost be touched from either side, ris ing rough, ragged, forbidding, nearly 4,000 feet above; not a tree, not a leaf in sight—nothing but many-hued granite and seething water, the whole made more terrible by the roar of the irein, echoed from cliff to cliff."

text: THREE GRAND Mourrams.—The mountains I now speak of are three in number, running nearly north and south; they connect one portion of the Drackenberg with another, but each stands separate and at almost equ distances apart; their altitude, I am told, is 9000 feet; which peak is the highest it would be difficult to say, for they are not equally dis tant from where we are now halted. The first and nearest has its sides, in fact all three have, at exactly the same angle, but the summit of each is crowned most dissimilarly. The nearest possesses for its apex a castle, and such a castle l not unlike that of Edinburgh, but increased in size a hundredfold. There are battlements and tower and watchhouse, and all so perfect that it is not necessary to draw upon imagination to believe them the works of man in the feudal ages ; and the sky is so clear, so rarified, that the outline of each detail of this immense citadel can be seen without aid of telescope. The summit of the second is a perfect representation of a crown, not such an is now worn on State occa sions by our most gracious Majesty, but such as you see in aged drawings as the headgear of warlike kings nine or ten centuries ago— men who competed with their lords and barons , who should be first to hew down the op posing foe. The third mountain is capped with a mitre ; it is not so perfect as the others, being rather broad in proportion to its height, such as might be expected to have come from the hands of an inexperienced workman, or that had suffered through some secrilegimes infidel having sat on it. Still it is a mitre. Thus we find capping three adjoining mountains a castle, crown, and mitre. Strange, wondrous strange. coincidence !—Parker Gilenore's Ride through Natal, 4-o. text: TRIPS TO MILFORD.—The presence of the Great Eastern and the Channel Fleet at Milford has had a completely magnetic influence upon the population of Merthyr and the hill districts. During the whole week they have been streaming down to see the " big ship" and the wooden walls of old England; and the morning coaches from 'Brecon, Tredegar, &c., have regularly arrived heavily laden with passengers, en route for Mil ford. There was a cheap excursion on Saturday even ing to return on Monday night; and a large num ber of persons, occupying eighteen carriages, availed themselves of the opportunity. They left Merthyr at 6 p.m., and arrived as Milford at half-past twelve; and at that late hour had to hunt up such sleeping accommoda tion as the place and neighbourhood afforded. text: The coachman of Lord Hastings, on Wednesday week, was directed to drive a gentleman from his Lordship's residence at Melton Constable to the railway terminus at Norwich, a distance of about 20 miles. He arrived at Norwich perfectly safe, and the gentleman proceeded by the next train to London. The coach man, whose name is Haylett, is a married man, and has a wife and young family living at Lenwade, a village about midway from Mel ton to Norwich. Having no one to drive back, instead of staying at Norwich all night with his carriage and horses, he determined to go as far as his wife's cottage and stay there, putting up his horses at Lenwade Bridge Inn. Unfortunately for him he did not keep himself sober in Norwich, and started from the Norfolk Hotel, in a somewhat questionable state, about 11 o'clock at night. After he passed the Drayton toll-gate, about five miles on the road, he appears to have fallen asleep, and the horses turned into aby lane, which ultimately led Into a field. Here thty seem to have wandered about, with Haylett sleeping on the box, the track of the wheels the next morning showing that the carriage, on one occasion, passed within a few inches of the edge of a deep marl pit, into which it seemed almost miraculous that they did not all fall. However, they found their way out of the field again, the coachman probably awaking. Thence they took a direction for Hingland, and attempted to ford a wide watering of the Wensum, but the immensely flooded state of the lowlands had given a great impetuosity to the stream, and they were carried away by it. At this time also Haylett appears to have been asleep upon the driv ing box, and when he awoke, about four o'clock in the morning, he found himself in the midst of these extensive waters, both the horses being drowned, awl the carriage severed, the fore from the hind wheels. We need hardly say he was dreadfully frightened; his screams brought up in a short time some of the watch from the game pi eserves of Mr. N. Micklethwaite, who rendered all the assistance they could. In the course of the morning the horses were got out, and the carriage also. Haylett was now in the greatest distress, and would probably have done himself some mis chief but for the police, who strictly guarded him. He was taken to the Bridge Inn, at Lenwade, and thence driven home to Melton to tell his gad tale. The horses were very valuable, his Lord ship having a few days before been offered 4150 for one.

text: The main line of the Highland Railway, continu. tag northway from Ballinluig, passes along the valley of the Tummel, in which is situated Pi;- 'ochry, the chief of the great summer resorts on the southern part of the line. Tourists will find the hest of hotels and hydropathics here, and many beautiful excursions, both driving and on ' foot, may be enjoyed from Pitlochry as a centre. The difficulty of deciding on the most beautiful scene in the Highland. is no small one; but cer tainly the Pass of Killicrankie has good claims to first place. and it is doubtful if there is a stretch of railway line three miles in length in any part of the British Islands that can hold its own with the three miles between Pitlochry and the tunnel at Killienrankie. At Blair-Atholl visitors will find excellent hotel a.ocommodatien, and those who are inter ested in Highland history will be delighted with a visit to Blair Castle, the seat of the Duke of Atholl, to which they are admitted between the hours of 9 a.m. and 6 p.m., on signing their names in a book, and on payment of one shilling each to a guide, who wik aceompany them. An interest ing drive or walk may be enjoyed from Blair- Atholl to the Falls of Bruer. (3 miles). Leaving BlainAtholl, the train commences the long, steep climb across the Grampian Mountains. For 16 miles the Highland enginee have to grapple with the hardest task allotted to any British loco motives, the line rising ultimately to a height of 1,484 feet a short. way beyond Dalnaspidal Station, the highest point reached on any railway system in the Kingdom. At Struan Station thew passengers who are going to Kinloch.Rannoeh leave the train and join the coach or obtain private carriages for the drive of 13 miles. At Newtonnow. 69 miles from Perth. thc train reaches the first of the famous summer resorts north of the Grampians. King-made, about three miles north, has for long been famous for its climate, the beauty of the district, and the ex oellence of its accommodation. From Knagussie for a distance of over 70 miles to Inverness, there is a succession of small towns. The Forces dis trict is full of interest and beauty. Here else Highland line turns east and west. At Kinloas, three miles from Forces, there are the interesting ruins of an old abbey. A few miles from Kinloss and about seven miles from Forres there is a charming little summer resort at the tillage of Findhorn, situated on the Moray Firth. text: The special correspondent of the Daily News, writing from the head quarters of the Modoc expedi tion, California, on the Ist inst., gives interesting details of the operations of the United States troops against the Modoc Indians. He says :—When I left San Francisco for the War Trail, I was in a state of almost complete ignorance about the Modoc war. As I moved north by train up the magnificent valley of the Sacraments, the cry for vengeance upon Captain Jack and all his tribe was at the highest. Some of the Indians wished that Captain jack had a hundred lives, and that they might be allowed to take them all. All kinds of terrible tortures were talked of. At Redding, about 300 miles from San Francisco, the railway ends, and we had to go by stage coach through the valleys where the Sacramento river rises. The first stoppage to breakfast was at one of those primi tive log-houses of an early settler. Near this place I met, for the first time in my life, a real Indian chief on what I might term his "native heath." He was the chief of the 11`Leod Indians; so named now from the MLLeed river, which here joins the Pit river, both tributaries of the Sacramento. His Indian name was " Ochoolooly," but he is generally called M‘Leod, and Capt. M‘Leod ; ih fact, he is "the M‘Leod of 11PLeod" of that part of the world. How unlike the Indian Chief of one's boyish reading! All the war paint and feathers are wanting. A wide-awake hat ; a flannel shirt served at the same time for coat and vest; dirty cotton trousers, held tight at the waist by a belt ; a pair of deer-skin mocassins on his feet being all that was left of the old costume. His daily occupation seemed to be that of coming to meet the coach, and beg tobacco. He spoke almost no English, but he had a half-caste Indian boy with him to do all the talking, and made enquiries as to whether we had any tobacco to give. We could see the Wickieups, or huts, of his family on the other side of the M‘Leod River. These forms of domestic architec ture are of a very primitive kind. They are made of sticks, mats, and straw, not unlike an inverted bird's nest, but most birds generally construct a much more comfortable kind of habitation. Going along we saw these Indians at the various ranches; many of them being employed as servants. The M‘Leod may be taken as a fair type of them all as they exist at the present day. They are usually dressed in cast-off clothes of the whites, and it is the same with the women. Their language is peculiar, and I had diffi culty at times in comprehending their meaning. Their principal peculiarity is the use of an enormous amount of profane swearing. Seventy-five per cent. of their words are oaths of the strongest kind; no matter what they speak about, it is all pre faced and concluded by old sacred and eccle siastical phrases. It is a style of talking which had its origin in the strange mass of humanity which first came to the country in the digging days. I asked one of them if there was any Act of Congress making it a penalty if they spoke with out accompaning it by oaths. "Well," he said, "it's a bad custom, but we are all so long given to the habit that we cannot get over it." They were nearly all familiarly acquainted with every man in the Modoc camp; and, strange to say, the feeling for vengeance, so strong in other parts, was not so manifest here. Many of these rough men spoke in defence of the Indians, and I heard of the frequent injustice which the !dodoes had suffered.

She, in order to satisfy the importunity of her sister, and under the idea, esultiug from the representations made to her that she was going to consult an eminent medical man, was induced to enter a coach, and being thus entrapped, was carried off and placed as a pauper lunatic in the Macclesfield Asylum. She was there through the influence of this sister detained long after the me4ical officer had reported that she was not a fit subject for the asylum, aud when in consequence of the interference of friends she was released, she found that during her confinement her furniture and stock in trade had been disposed of by public auction, and that she herself was left in a state of absolute and utter destitution. The assistance of friends alone prevented her becoming for the first time in her life dependent for the means of existence on the parish. The Committee repeat their regret that the public official inquiry has not been granted ; the real facts of the case would then have been ascertained, and the disregard of the law, if proved have been duly and authoritatively condemned.—l am, sir, yours most obediently. text: WE are aware that a curious and yet very interesting result of the bicycle and tricycle has been the revival of many of the old country inns. The old roadside hotels that flourished in the coaching days and seem since to have been almost deserted. The old inns associated with many a story of the road, the kind jinn that Mr. Pickwick and Mr. Weller stayed at on their way down to Bath. All these places, or but too many of them, seem to have fallen into a kind of lethargy since the stage coach and the stag e wagon disappeared, and have been forgotten. Steam and the iron horse rush across the country, and the sound of the horn, the jingle of harness, and the clatter of hoofs no longer resound along the high roads. The old inn appeared to have died of inani• tion, but it is not so. After a sleep as long as that of Rip Van Winkle, they have come or are coming to life again; and as it was the iron horse and steam that sent them into that long lethargy, it is the new iron horse and his rider that have revived them. Our valiant youth, rejoicing in their strength and possessing doubtless a good share of exploring and wandering instinct that is bred in our bones, and descended; in us no doubt from the Vikings, determined to ex plore the country from Lands End to John o' Groats, and from the Severn to the Tyne. Along every high road and bye-road the ring of the warning bell has been heard, until even the peasant in remote places no longer flees away in terror to tell his old woman how he had " seen a chap riding upo' nothin' " when a bicycle comes his way. And, as a very natural consequence of the extent of these wanderings, of the popularity of the sport, and of the very large number of cycle clubs and their ex cursions, the old inns have come in fora large share of the new custom. Pedestrians have always had a reputation for faunas appetites at the end of their journey, andif pedestrians, a fortiori cyclists, who are always hungry, and thirsty, and tired whoa they reach their hotel at last. The cyclists then have found the old inns, with their great grass grown court yards and their large low roofed dining rooms, not only comfortable and convenient but quaint and homely. So they have naturally resorted back to them, and the old places hare bloomed and freshened under their patron age. We are clad of it. We know new cr, • inventions must come and must dislocate old notions and old associations, and destroy lovely old spots and nooks and dells, where as boys, we used to play; but, all the same, one cannot help regretting that it mug be, so, and one dislikes to see the signs of deaf that were lately so palpable among the °id road-side hostelries. We are glad to see they are likely to have a new lease of life, and what may easily be a permanent lease. That is now 25 to 30 years ago, an d robin teeringc;ies inisoo tocv fa n n •an d fi:;ed than ever, and in i r popular. Now sve have ono her generation, and with it the eyeli and wonderf,ll wanderings over the laud ami in stranw places. text: WHAT A GENTLEMAN MAY DO, AND WHAT HE MAY NOT DO.—He niay carry a brace of partridges, but not a leg of mutton. He may be seen in the omnibus-box at the opera, but not on the box of an omnibus. He may be seen in a kali inside a theatre, but not at a stall outside one. He may dust another person's jacket, but must not brush his own. He may kill a man in a duel, but he musnt't eat peas with his knife. He may thrash a coalheaver, but he musnt't ask twice for soup. He may pay his debts of honour, but he need nottrouble himself about his tradesmen's bills. He may drive a stage coach, but he mustn't take or carry cop pers. He may ride a horse as a jockey, but he mustn't exert himself in the least to get his living. He must never forget what he owes to himself as a gentleman, but he need not mind what he owes as a gentleman to his tailor. He may do anything, or anybody, in fact within the range of a gen tleman—go through the Insolvent Debtor's Court, or turn billiard-marker; but he must never on any account carry a brown paper parcel, or appear in the streets without a pair of gloves.—Comic Ahnanaek. FORETHOUGHT AND SAGACITY OF RATEI.—III Gutting through an embankment in a field adjoining the river Lune the other day, for the formation of one of the culverts ren dered necessary by the passing of the North-Western Rail way in that direction, the labourers met with between 15lb and 201 b of eels, some quite fresh, and others in the last stage of putrefaction. They varied from a quarter to half a pound in weight, and consisted of the common silver-bel lied, or river eel, and Lilliputian specimens of the conger, or sea eel. The latter, of course, had come up with the tide. As teeth marks were visible on the heads of most of them, it was conjectured they had been destroyed in that way, and stored for winter provision, by some animal whose retreat was not far distant. This proved to be the case. On digging aiittle further out bounced a matronly rat, with seven half-grown young ones at her heels. The work men gave chase, and ultimately succeeded in killing both mother and progeny, with a solitary exception, the trunk of a neighbouring tree affording an asylum to one of the family. The embankment is about 100 yards from the wa ter's edge, so that it must have required considerable time and labour on the part of the old rat to have dragged the eels thither.—Lancas er Guardian. - •

The number of trains must be reduced, especially on long lines. * • 5 Long lines have a better chance of recovering themselves than short, and would be the first to feel the benefits of improved man agement and better times. Short lines, if they are to run frequent trains, should use composite carriages and light engines. Their heavy engines should be reserved for their goods traffic, if they have any, and for extraordinary occa sions. To run two or three first-class carriages for half-a dozen first-class passengers, as we have seen, and drawn by a Goliath of an engine, is the height of folly. Economy re quires that the means should be appropriate to the end, the power to the work to be done. If it is not so the ex penses are d isproportioned to the income, and reduced profits or loss will be the consequence. Assuming the management otherwise honest, it is obvious that the future prosperity of railways centres in two things—the fair letting of their con tracts by public tender, and a judicious reduction of the number of their trains on long lines, and the running of light engines and composite carriages on short lines. A reduction of the trains to one-half will not halve the Company's ex penses, but it will go a long way towards it. If the expenses could be reduced to two-thirds, there are very few lines that would not pay a good dividend. Indeed, we feel confident that this is the true and only road left to prosperity. It is in the great items the savings must be made, and net in little meannesses. If the reductions be applied in the proper quar ters, possibly there would be no reason to raise the tariffs. text: Why does a dog walk round in a little circle before lying down? Because his ancestors had to beat out a hole in the grass or the snow to make a bed. Why does he lay his nose on his paws? Because his ances tors had to keep their noses clear of the dust or snow. Why does a cat wash herself so carefully? Because her ancestors had to be clean or their prey would smell them, and thus escape. Instances could be given by thousa.nds of ancient habits still pre served by animals long after they have ceased to be useful. Yet man does exactly the same thing without knowing it—preserves innumerable habits for centuries after they have ceased to have any meaning. Why are there two buttons on the back of a man's coat? Because our ancestors needed them as rests for their sword belts. Look at a corner-post now, and you will see that it is shaped and banded like the old cannon at street corners, with a half-ball on top in memory of the round-shot in the muzee. Look at any iron railing. The posts are shaped like spears, shaft and tip, in memory of some forgotten weapon, almost certain to be the spear, largely used in the Middle Ages. Our railway carriages to-day are imi tations of the stage coach; and our carpets nearly all have a flower pat tern, for in ancient days the floors . were strewn with rushes, interspersed on State occasions with living flowers. Hence man's innumerable whims.—T. Ewing, Seamer, Scarborough.

There being a great number of wooden patterns inside, the flames spread very rapidly, and in a remarkably short time the entire building was a mass of ruins. We are unable to learn the amount of loss sustained, but it is stated that the firm is insured. It may be mentioned that, about three years ago, the same gentlemen had their foundry burnt down. Housebreaking and Apprehension of the Thief. —About two o'clock on Wednesday morning, while one of the watchmen at the west end of the town was going his rounds, he ob served a man lurking about a wright's shop in the vicinity of the Royal Crescent, who seemed anxious to screen him self from observation. This aroused the suspicions of the officer, and he immediately advanced towards the man, who was crouching in a corner under the shadow the wall, and observed that he had a large basket along with him. When ever the person saw that he was discovered, he made a bolt to escape, and the watchman pursued; but opportunely at this moment another officer turned the corner of the street, and captured him. On examining the basket, it was found to contain a large quantity of tools belonging to the work men in the shop, to the value of upwards of £lO. The brig Rebecca, Captain Simpson, arrived in the Clyde on Tuesday last, with six of the sufferers of the wreck of the ship Amity, of Liverpool, taken off by the schooner Jenny Lind. These poor men were three days and nights in the mizen chains without food. The River Bailie very kindly gave admission to two of them into the Royal Infirmary, their feet being badly frost-bitten, and the men had to be conveyed in a coach. The other four have been assisted and forwarded by the Shipwrecked Mariner's Society to Liverpool. We cannot but feel thankful to the whole of the Liverpool and Glasgow Steam Packet Co.'s for their kindness in assisting the good endeavours of this Society, by granting all shipwrecked mariners a free iassage in their steamers. Fatal Occurrence.—On the 12th inst., a young man, named Edward Harkins, lost his life in Mr. Arbuckle's tanyard, Cartsdyke, Greenock, under peculiar circumstances. He and a companion were suspectedof setting fire to a hay and a corn stack, on the farm of Finnieston, and the police were search ing for them. In order to escape their vigilance, the two lads got into the tan-yard in the evening, and lay down in the bark store under a loft filled with that material. About an hour or two after going in, a large part of the bark slid down upon them, fixing them firmly by the shoulders and arms. They struggled hard to effect their escape, but ineffectually, as towards morning the elder lad, Harkins, became exhausted, and was suffocated. His companion was discovered in the morning by the lad who had admitted them, and was rescued in time to prevent his death, although he also was nearly gone. His being saved was owing to his having lain down under the steps of a ladder leading to the upper part of the store, and thus some fresh air was admitted to him, while his less fortunate companion was lying over the steps. He was alive a long time after the bark fell, as the two lads were able to communicate with each other, and the younger one thinks the other lived till about an hour before he him self was rescued.

This is an aspect of Christmas festivity which is the monopoly of no class, for as Dickens wrote—and no one ever wrote more tenderly on such a subject— Th. ties that bind the wealthy and the proud to home may be forged on earth, but those which link the poor man to his humble hearth are of the true metal, and bear the stamp of heaven." It seems therefore as though a special providence had ordained the winter festival, and it is hard to imagine what the long winter would be without it, although of late years our real winters have certainly been for the most part after Christmas has gone by. In the depth of winter all, or nearly all, outdoor pastimes are at a dead-lock, and home is decidedly the best if not the only resort. In former times it was next to im possible to get far away from it, and even now it is someimes neither easy nor pleasant. Here again we have advanced a stage or two in this utilitarian age. The worst-warmed and lighted third-class railway carriage is less cold and uncomfortable at such a time tian the top of a coach, and what may be slow for a train would nevertheless be quick travelling on the road. So late as 1835 all the Exeter and London coaches were stopped by snow on the borders of Salisbury plain. The Bishop of Exeter, the Earl of Devon, and several west country M.P.'s were among the passengers, but the whole week were they forced to remain at a standstill, and that occasion, at all events, never saw them in their places at the opening of Parliament. The Christmas of 1836 was also one to be re membered by travellers. The Devonport mail, for the greater part of the journey, had to turn on two leaders ridden post, on account of the height of the snowdrifts, which would have turned any horses driven in the ordinary way. The Birmingham mail got embedded in the snow near Aylesbury, and the passengers had to make their way on foot to any shelter they could find. On the same day the Holyhead and Chester mails came to grief within a few yards of each other, in the background being a postchaise, from one of the windows of which an elderly and terrified female shrieked for speedy deliverance, the postboys having gone off with the horses in search of assistance. The centralising tendency of our Govern ment has lately so manifested itself in the provi sions and requirements of the Merchants' Ship ping Act, that an attempt is being made to have its evils removed. The chief ground of complaint is the arbitrary and one-sided proceedings which the Board of Trade take against captains and officers of ships meeting with accident. Not only are they obliged to Submit to a sort of trial, but before the case is heard, the certificate is im pounded, thereby prejudging the case, and deny ing to the accused what is granted to the most atrocious criminal—a fair and impartial hearing. The constitution of the court is also faultg in the extreme. It is generally composed of a naval officer and a local magistrate, gentlemen who, in nine cases out of ten, know nothing of the 'subject' they have to investigate. If a peer of the realm is tried for any alleged offence against the laws of the country, ,his case is adjudicated upon by a jury of his peers. If an officer in the navy or the - army is charged with any breach of duty, he stands a court-martial, where his brother officers are his jury, If a laWyer is struck off the Rolls, he has first had his case enquired into, and in none of these instances does the punishment precede the trial. Towards the captains of our mercantile marine; a different sort or justice is administered. To him the certificate of the Marine Board is' equivalent to an officer's corn commission in the army or navy. The moment the investigation commences, that instant does the Board of Trade require him to hand up his, certificate. Without it he cannot proceed to sea, and serious consequences to both the, captain ' and owners of the ship are often the result. Recently both our representatives anirnad• verted upon the arbitrary conduct of the Board 'of Trade, and'pointed out the highly objection able character of its constitution. A noble Peer, who boasts of an ancient, though perhaps not distinguished ancestry, but whose pride it is to boast that he was never engaged in trade, is scarcely fit for the head of so important a depart mentofthe Government, and an Australian lawyer or a superannuated Indian J udge are scarcely to be expected to afford any more valuable aid in _forming the National Council for directing and controlling matters appertaining to trade, com merce, or finance, These gentlemen may all be very estimable and even able gentlemen in their way ; but it by no means follows that because the one is a Peer, and the others second-rate lawyers, that they are competent to direct the destinies of the Board of Trade. It was only on the receipt of a wire from the station master at Oxenholme Junction, announcing the arrival of a certain number of persons for Ambleside, that a coach ever met that particular train, and it happened that that evening Harry Marsden was the only person in the train, which was a purely local one, who was going on from Winder mere. There was nothing for it but to walk the five mites, because it was quite out of the question that he should take a private carriage. The Bank only allowed the half-crown for coach fair, and Harry was much too enonomical to spend one penny of his own money on behalf of his employers. Accordingly, rather pleased at having saved a half crown, and not at all depressed at the prospect of a walk along one of the most charming roads in England, he sot out for Ambleside. Ho was not in the least nervous en account of the large sum of money he had about him. The worst that he had to fear was the nio:!t ing of some wretched tramp, and he felt more than prepared to cope with any such that might interfere with him on his way home. On account of his handsome face, his high spirits, and his love of adventure, he was made the boon companion of a set of men who lived handsomely on their wits and other people's wealth. Among them was the son of a country clergyman, an unsuccessful actor, an Irish soldier, and a gipey vagabond. Boris's right IMMO was Stephens, and he belonged to a family of yeomen peculiar to the North—sturdy, law abiding and industrious—devout Presbyterians, whose strongest motive in life is to maintain the tenant right of tilster, which secures to them a settled tenure in their land, and a freedom from the tyranny that oppresses their Catholic brethren in the south. For thirty years the Earl of Leitrim had been at strife with his tenants— he had 90,000 acres of land, stretching across three counties, and giving him a rental of over £9OOO per annum, and he spent the best part of this in harassing his poorer neighbours by suits at law but the worst trait was shown in his attempts to dishonour the wives and daughters of his tenants, and to accomplish this his influence as a peer and a magistrate and his power as a landlord was used without fear or restraint. Hugh Stephens had served in the British Army for five years, and with an excellent record us a soldier. On his return home he rented a email place and commenced life as a farmer. One day he met his landlord driving on the road and was ordered to ditch his little cart so as to make room for the peer's coach. This command was enforced with a horsewhip, and resented with a cudgel, the earl getting much the worst of it. This was the beginning of trouble for Stephens —he was evicted and ruined by litigation, and his sister, a beautiful and intelligent girl, was assaulted by a ruffianly retainer of his land lord and her character assailed. Some of the neigh bouring gentry took this up, the man was arrested, tried, and sentenced to ten years' imprisonment. Leitrim was furious, and swore vengeance on all con cerned. In March, 1878, a dozen of the tenantry met at a rath in the mountains overlooking Lough Foyle. One of the oldest and most respected of the men on the estate said a few words to the effect that the tvranny of their landlord was more than they could endure, and it was now necessary to resort to the last means in their power to preserve their lives 1 and the honour of their daughters and wives, and all swore to be true to the cause in life or death; £9O was raised. It was resolved to act at once, and six men were chosen as the instruments of justice. They had brought themselves to believe that in the removal of a tyrant they were doing right. Stephens was their leader, and he pro cured the necessary arms. One of their most active and trusted agents was a woman servant at Castle Leitrim; her sister had been brutally treated by the earl, and it was her revenge to keep the assassins fully informed of their victim's movements. On April 2 he left Manor Vaughan to go to Milford, en route to ' Londonderry. He was attended by a bailiff named Meehan, who sat on the car by his side, with the driver in front. There was a second car containing his valet and another bailiff. All were well armed. The day was beautiful, but rather misty. Stephens and his party stationed themselves behind a clump of low thorn trees, close to the road, armed with double-barrelled guns. From the roof of a cabin 400 yards away on the hillside a white cloth was displayed.. This was the signal that the earl was coming. His indifference to danger was mani fested by the manner in which he divided his party. The second car was 100 yards away, and entirely hidden by a hollow in the road. A short time before Lord Leitrim bad evicted a woman named Algoe, and opposite her ruined cabin he fell. Three of the party had been soldiers, and were good shots, and each brought down his man. One of the guns, a rude weapon, buret, and blew the holder's thunib off. The driver was killed on the spot. The bailiff ran back to the hind car, and dropped dead in the road; but the earl was alive when his enemies surrounded him. When making an effort to draw his pistol he received three loads of swan shot in the body, and when the party behind came up he was dead, and save the ruins of the gun and an old horse pistol nothing was left to indicate the identity of his slayer.. Nor were they ever traced. Two of the criminals died in Australia, two in the Boer War in South Africa, while Stephens came to this conntry and lived a blameless life until he died. Eight year. ago, according to our Transatlantic centeniperary, he gave this narrative, intended to monera:e another man, and with the stipulation that it be kept secret until after his death, and now, for the first time, the remarkable story is published. How far it is true, we cannot say.

Resuming my account of the old road,in bygone days a short halt was made at Warrington, which is nearly equi-distant between Liverpool and Manchester, for refreshments and to change horses. The Ta bo t and the Nag's Head are the two inns mentioned in Mr. Weblis careful guide of 1822,but some custom went to the' others. Taking the figures as Mr. Webb gives them, it would seem that in the Liverpool coaches 120 horses must have been changed daily. The country which the coaches ' ran through from Warrington to Prescot is excel ently suited for the par pose from its flatness. I•ara told by those who were in the habit of going to Liverpool in coaching days that snowstorms did not cause much inconvenience. This was a great trouble not only in hilly districts but in the eastern counties when snowstorms of great violence swept over the country from the North Sea. In one of his happiest moments Dickens describes a storm that he actually was in on his road to the Nortk. This is in "Nicholas Nickleby," in the fifth chapter :—" The night and the snow came on together, and dismal enough they were. There was no sound to be heard but the howling of the wind, for the noise of the wheels and the tread of the horses' feet were rendered inaudible by the thick coating of snow which covered the earth and was fast increasing every moment. The streets of Stamford were deserted as they passed through the town, and its old churches rose frowning and dark from the whitened ground." The upset of the coach ia the snow half way between Grantham and Newark is a record of an adventure that had re cently happened to Dickens. The great snowstorm of 1836, which commenced in the North of England, cer tainly impeded the mails for a few hours, but that was a trifle te what occurred in the South. Coaches were abandoned on the road, and some were stopped for a whole night, blocked up within a few miles,from London. For two days London was shut off from a great part Of England. The Manchester gown mail only reached of. Albans, where it was blooked•And afterwards upset, and the guard returned to London with the mails. A Western papersays of Manchester—" The principal roads which have been rendered for a time impassable are the roads to Sheffield by Glossop and the Woodlands, the London road in the south of Warwickshire, also between dshbourne and Derby " • but the roads to the west of Manchester were, it said, "free from any considerable obstruction." . The railway between Liverpool and Manchester, which was °petted In September, 1830, had so astonished the public with its 'access, that it was clear the days of coaching were numbered; yet in 1831 a perfect host of new coaches started from Manchester to London, princi pally owned by John Knowles, and the Peacock, the Royal Hotel, and the Swan were for a time the scenes ef great activity. Warrington, which forms such a happy centre between the two great cities lies in the hundred of West Derby. Mr. John Ireland tila:okburne was formerly lord of the manor, but now that dignity belongs to the Corporation. According to Emerson, the first stage coach In England was started here, and here the first Lancashire newspaper was printed. Howard's work on prisons was printed here, and many other notable books came from the press of the Eyres. From Warrington the coach road passes by Hatton Hall, which has been a pleasant residence in its time, but it is now a farm house. A labourer lives at the lodge, and the bow win dows of the drawing-room look over haystacks and a farmyard. This is by the Sankey Brook navigation, which was opened in 1755. The road has lost much even of the artificial interest that belonged to it, such as old houses and trees. It is now lined with works and work men's cottages. About three miles from Warrington it reaches the lodges of Bold Hall. This is one of the state ly mansions of Lancashire, and is situated in a park about two miles in length, if we take it from the War rington road to the Burtonwood road. The hall was built in the early part of last century, and is a noble example of Italian architecture as made to do duty in England. The place is very commodious and artistic. For some time the hall has been empty, though it would seem to be a tempting residence. There is a careful oil p aint ing left of the old Bold Hall among ths family archives, and it would seem to have been a splendid specimen of black-and=whife architecture. There was a moat round it, and Dr. Leigh gives an interesting account of the wild fowl there. The wild ducks were numerous in all South Lancashire, and bred on marshy ponds. and morasses. They especially favoured such places as Bold, where there were keepers. Rainhill, which is next reached, has some traces of picturesqueness, but its in tiquities have vanished. Prescot, the birthplace of John Kemble, is well situated on high ground,and looks rather picturesque as we approach it, but the town has little interest. The church, which is a valuable living, is quite a wreck, and has no antiquity left. Soon after leaving Prescot we reach a succession of finely built mansions, which extend for some five miles out of Liver pool, and are in well-kept grounds. They had come there to strike a song of hop— n song which he trusted would be an inspiration to the industrial army of this country. They had seen gradually, but nevertheless surely, the condition of the worker growing worse and worse and they now heard the most Ominous sound that could strike the ear of the middle-aged man : "Too old at forty." text: • • Last Bank Holiday . 1 referred to the fact that the plot of land which the Local Board propose to acquire for a recreation ground was crowded all the afternoon. The same may be said of Monday. There can be no doubt about this—that to inland people the attraction is the sea, and in West Kirby this is about the only piece which commands a full view of the sea. But I am told by a gentleman, who ought to know, that to acquire this plot of land, and a similar plot at Hoylake, would add 4d. in the £ to the already heavy rates. I think I was one of the first to press upon the Board the advisability of acquiring this piece of laud, but I confess that I never suspected the cost would be so heavy. The question will have to be faced, for I believe the West Kirby improvement Committee has decided to ask every ratepayer to vote upon the question. Most ratepayers will shrink from such an addition to the rates I fancy, although there can be no question about the value of the plot. S . I hear that the scheme for converting the swampy ground behind the Wesleyan Chapel, West Kirby, into a lake is making satisfactory progress. There was a nasty accident to a cyclist at the foot of Orange Hill, West Kirby, on Mon. day afternoon. Coming down the hill, the young man seems to have lost control of his machine, with the result that he came to grief at the bottom. He was thrown off at the turn at the foot of the hill, and his throat was so badly cut by falling upon the wall of Mr. Lea's garden that Dr. King had to be called in. It is a great wonder the hill is not labelled "dangerous." It is worthy of note that the accident happened at the same place as the coach accident which was recorded in this column a few months ago. I have seen bicy clists come down this hill at a speed which showed how little was their regard for their own or other people's safety. Such accidents should teach riders a lesson. On Tuesday morning a lad, who had driven his machine from Chester, came into unpleasant contact with a cart at the foot of this same hill. The machine was badly damaged, and the lad placed in a very awkward position. He could not walk back to-Cheater, and he had'ut any money for a railway fare. After a good deal of trouble his machine was patched up, and he started the return journey. Whether he reached home or not is a mystery to me.

text: • • • On Thursday morning Mr Andrew Carnegie, the American millionaire, accompanied by Mrs Carnegie and a party numbering eleven, including Mr and Mrs Blaine, started from the Hotel Metropole, London, on a coaching trip. The destination of the I party is Cluny Castle, in the far north of 'Scotland, the home of the Macpbersons, which Mr Carnegie has leased. Mr Black, the novelist, was invited to join the party, but was unable to make such a long trip. The coach stopped on Thursday evening at Hertford. The journey will be made leisurely; the distance overtaken each day being limited to 25 miles. Mr Carnegie is in high spirits, and he expects his friends will have a happy and a useful holiday in the North. It is prob able that Mr Carnegie will remain in thil country for about four months.
